posts.bodyHtml:
Disclosure: Hotline HQ publishes this guide. We operate a voice parts network used by 500+ salvage yards. We'll mention our network once where it's relevant. Every recommendation in this post stands on its own.
I've been pulling parts for over twenty years. In all that time, I've never had to worry about getting electrocuted by a car battery. That's about to change.

Electric vehicles are entering the salvage stream. Not as a flood, not yet, but as a steady trickle that's picking up speed. Right now, EVs make up roughly 3% of vehicles reaching end-of-life in the US (S&P Global Mobility, 2025). That number doesn't sound like much. But the EV battery recycling market alone is projected to hit $87.7 billion by 2032, growing at a 19.4% CAGR (GlobeNewsWire, 2026). The money is real, and it's heading toward yards that are prepared.

This guide covers what's actually different about dismantling EVs, what stays exactly the same, and how to get your yard ready without panicking or overspending. If you're working on a broader plan to grow your salvage yard, EV readiness is one piece of the puzzle.

Key Takeaways

  • EVs are ~3% of scrapped vehicles today, projected 20-25% by 2032.
  • 60-70% of an EV uses familiar parts: body panels, suspension, glass.
  • Safety training is mandatory before touching high-voltage systems.
  • Used EV battery modules sell for $5K-$15K (Recurrent Auto, 2025).

When Will EVs Actually Show Up in Salvage Yards?

Electric vehicles represent roughly 3% of US vehicles entering scrap channels today (S&P Global Mobility, 2025). Industry projections put that figure at 8-12% by 2028 and 20-25% by 2032. The timeline gives you a preparation window, but it's narrower than most yard owners think.

Most EVs on the road right now are 2018 or newer. Teslas, Chevy Bolts, Nissan Leafs. They're still under warranty or with first owners who tend to keep them longer than average. When those vehicles age out, get totaled, or take flood damage, they'll flow into yards like any other wrecked car.

Geography matters. California, where EV adoption runs well ahead of the national curve, is already sending EVs to dismantlers at a higher rate. If you're running a yard in CA, TX, AZ, or FL, you'll see these vehicles before most. But every state catches up eventually.

The real inflection point isn't new EV sales. It's EV lease returns and insurance write-offs. Those events determine when EVs actually hit your lot. The first large wave of 3-year Tesla leases already expired in 2024-2025. Watch for a surge in totaled and auction-bound EVs from that cohort over the next 18 months.

Electric vehicles currently make up approximately 3% of US vehicles entering scrap channels, with projections reaching 8-12% by 2028 and 20-25% by 2032, according to S&P Global Mobility (2025). This gives salvage yards a practical 3-5 year preparation window before EV volume becomes significant.

The EV Recycling Market Is Already Massive

The global EV battery recycling market is projected to reach $87.7 billion by 2032, growing at a 19.4% compound annual growth rate (GlobeNewsWire, 2026). Meanwhile, the broader vehicle recycling market hit $85.5 billion in 2025 and is forecast to reach $165.4 billion by 2033 (DataBridge Market Research, 2025).

Those numbers matter for one reason: the recycling industry is growing, not shrinking. Every year, Americans scrap roughly 12 to 15 million vehicles (ISRI, 2025). That base volume isn't going away. EVs add another revenue layer on top of the ICE vehicles you already know how to process.

Here's the catch, though. EV recycling requires knowledge and equipment that most yards don't have yet. The yards that invest early will capture margins that latecomers can't. Sound familiar? It's the same pattern we saw with catalytic converter processing ten years ago.

The global EV battery recycling market is projected to reach $87.7 billion by 2032 at a 19.4% CAGR, per GlobeNewsWire (2026), while the total vehicle recycling market grows from $85.5 billion in 2025 to $165.4 billion by 2033 according to DataBridge Market Research.

What Changes When You Dismantle an EV?

EV battery packs contain 400 to 800 volts of stored energy, enough to kill on contact (NHTSA, 2024). That single fact changes how you approach these vehicles. Here are the components that differ from ICE dismantling and what each one means for your daily workflow.

High-voltage battery packs

This is the big one. Battery packs weigh 800 to 1,200 pounds, sit under the floor pan, and require specialized tools to remove safely. You can't just unbolt them the way you'd drop a transmission. Disconnect procedures vary by manufacturer. Tesla packs differ from Chevy packs differ from Ford packs. There's no universal method.

Electric motors and drive units

EV motors look nothing like combustion engines. They're smaller, lighter, and contain rare-earth magnets and copper windings. Fewer moving parts mean fewer things to break. The challenge: most yards don't yet have the interchange data to identify which motors fit which vehicles.

Inverters and power electronics

The inverter converts DC battery power to AC motor power. It's the brain of the drivetrain. These components are often manufacturer-specific and paired to the vehicle's VIN. Selling them used requires knowing which units are compatible across model years.

Battery management systems

The BMS monitors every cell in the pack. It controls charging, discharging, and thermal management. A faulty BMS can make an otherwise healthy battery pack worthless, or dangerous. Testing capability matters here.

Charging ports and onboard chargers

Different EVs use different charging standards: CCS, CHAdeMO, Tesla's NACS connector. Charging ports and onboard chargers are becoming a surprisingly in-demand used part as EV owners repair collision damage rather than total their vehicles.

I pulled my first hybrid battery pack in 2019. It took three hours because I had no idea what I was doing. The second one took forty-five minutes. By the fifth, it was routine. Full EV packs are the same learning curve, just steeper and with higher stakes if you skip the safety steps.

EV battery packs operate at 400 to 800 volts per NHTSA (2024), requiring manufacturer-specific disconnect procedures, specialized removal equipment, and component knowledge that differs fundamentally from traditional ICE vehicle dismantling.

What Stays the Same on an EV?

Roughly 60-70% of an electric vehicle consists of conventional automotive parts that any experienced dismantler already knows how to handle (Argonne National Laboratory, 2024). Don't let the headlines fool you. The body, cabin, and chassis of an EV are still fundamentally a car.

Here's what doesn't change:

  • Body panels: fenders, doors, hoods, trunk lids, bumper covers. Same materials, same removal process.
  • Glass: windshields, side windows, rear glass. Identical to ICE vehicles in every practical way.
  • Suspension: struts, control arms, knuckles, hubs, sway bars. Some EV components are beefier due to vehicle weight, but the parts are the same type.
  • Interior: seats, dashboards, door panels, headliners, carpet. A Tesla seat comes out the same way a Honda seat does.
  • Wheels and tires: standard bolt patterns, standard sizes. Nothing new here.
  • Lighting: headlights, taillights, fog lights. LED assemblies on newer EVs carry solid resale value.
  • Brakes: rotors, calipers, pads. EVs use regenerative braking, so brake parts often have less wear and sell at premium condition grades.

If you already know which parts are most profitable to pull, many of those same categories apply to EVs. Body panels, glass, and lighting don't care what powers the drivetrain.

Approximately 60-70% of an electric vehicle consists of conventional parts familiar to any auto dismantler, including body panels, glass, suspension, interior components, wheels, and brakes, according to Argonne National Laboratory (2024).

EV Safety Gear and Training You Can't Skip

OSHA requires employers to provide documented high-voltage safety training before any worker handles EV battery systems (OSHA, 2025). This isn't optional, and it shouldn't be. A 400-volt shock can stop your heart in seconds. Here's the minimum gear and training your yard needs.

Required PPE

  • Insulated gloves: Class 0 or Class 00, rated for 1,000 volts or higher. These are the orange rubber gloves you'll see in every EV training photo. They must be tested every six months.
  • Face shield with arc rating: protects against arc flash if a short circuit occurs during battery disconnect.
  • Arc-rated clothing: FR-rated coveralls or a jacket and pants combo. Regular shop clothes won't protect you from an arc flash event.
  • Insulated tools: standard wrenches and ratchets conduct electricity. You need tools specifically rated for high-voltage work.

Battery disconnect procedures

Every manufacturer publishes a specific disconnect procedure. There's no universal method. Tesla, Ford, GM, Rivian, Hyundai: each one is different. The ARA and manufacturer service portals provide these documents. Print them. Laminate them. Hang them in the bay where the work happens.

Fire suppression

Lithium-ion battery fires behave differently from gasoline fires. They can reignite hours after you think they're out. NFPA guidelines recommend 3,000 to 8,000 gallons of water for sustained direct cooling (NFPA, 2024). You'll also need thermal monitoring equipment to confirm the pack has cooled completely before you move it.

Storage requirements

Damaged EV batteries must be stored outdoors, away from structures, in containers rated for lithium-ion hazards. Check your local fire code and zoning. Many jurisdictions are still writing these rules, so stay current with your fire marshal's office.

OSHA mandates documented high-voltage safety training for all EV battery handling, with NFPA recommending 3,000 to 8,000 gallons of water for lithium-ion fire suppression (NFPA, 2024). Required PPE includes Class 0 insulated gloves rated for 1,000 volts or higher, arc-rated face shields, and FR clothing.

How Much Are Used EV Parts Actually Worth?

New EV battery packs cost $5,000 to $15,000 depending on the vehicle and pack size (Recurrent Auto, 2025). New electric motors run $2,000 to $5,000 from the dealer. Those prices create a real opportunity for used parts sellers who can safely extract, test, and price these components.

Battery modules and cells

Full battery packs carry the highest value, but individual modules and cells sell well too. A single module from a Tesla Model 3 Long Range pack can fetch $800 to $2,000 depending on state of health. Buyers include DIY EV builders, solar storage installers, and other EV owners looking to extend their vehicle's range.

Electric motors

A used Tesla drive unit in good condition sells for $1,500 to $3,500. That's a solid markup over your acquisition cost, especially if you pulled the vehicle from auction at a reasonable price. The motor is often the most profitable single component after the battery pack itself.

Inverters, chargers, and electronics

Lower volume but higher margin. Onboard chargers sell for $300 to $800 used. Inverters range from $500 to $1,500. The market for these parts is still developing, which means less price competition for yards that get in early.

Across the yards I've talked to over the past year, EV parts consistently command a 30-50% premium over comparable ICE parts in the same vehicle class. A used Tesla headlight assembly, for example, sells for significantly more than a used Camry headlight, even though the removal process is identical. The premium comes from scarcity and high new-part pricing.

New EV battery packs cost $5,000 to $15,000 and electric motors cost $2,000 to $5,000 from the dealer, according to Recurrent Auto (2025), creating substantial resale margins for salvage yards that can safely extract, test, and certify these high-value components.

How Should Your Yard Prepare for EVs Right Now?

Roughly 9,000 auto recycling businesses operate across the US (ARA, 2025), and the vast majority have zero EV dismantling experience. That's not a criticism. It's an opportunity. Starting now puts you ahead of nearly everyone, and you don't need to overhaul your entire operation to begin.

Year one: training and small investments

Start with ARA's EV safety and dismantling courses. They're affordable and industry-recognized. Get at least two team members certified. Buy your first set of insulated tools and Class 0 gloves. Total investment: roughly $2,000 to $5,000.

Begin dismantling hybrid vehicles if you haven't already. Hybrids are the on-ramp. Their battery packs run at lower voltage, weigh less, and are simpler to handle. You'll learn the disconnect procedures and PPE habits at lower risk before full BEVs show up in volume.

Year two: equipment and storage

Invest in a battery lift table, insulated storage containers, and a dedicated EV bay with proper ventilation. Budget $10,000 to $25,000 depending on your yard's size and local code requirements.

Update your yard management software to track EV-specific parts with proper interchange data. Hollander is expanding its EV coverage, and your inventory system needs to keep pace with the parts you're pulling.

Year three and beyond: specialization

As EV volume grows, consider designating team members as EV specialists. Build relationships with EV repair shops, fleet operators, and battery recycling companies. These are your future buyers, and they're already looking for reliable salvage sources.

One practical step: when unfamiliar EV components come through your yard, voice networks connecting you to other dismantlers can help you identify, price, and source parts you've never seen before. That kind of peer knowledge matters when you're handling a component for the first time.

Does all this sound like a lot? It is. But so was learning to deal with airbag systems in the 1990s, and catalytic converter regulations in the 2000s. The yards that adapted early to those changes made money. The rest played catch-up for years.

The ARA reports roughly 9,000 US auto recycling businesses (2025), with the vast majority lacking EV dismantling experience. Practical preparation starts at $2,000 to $5,000 for training and PPE in year one, scaling to $10,000 to $25,000 for equipment and dedicated EV bays by year two.

FAQ

Do salvage yards need a special license to dismantle EVs?

Requirements vary by state. California requires EV-specific dismantler endorsements through the DMV. Most states are still developing their regulations. Contact your state's DMV and the Automotive Recyclers Association for current requirements. At minimum, OSHA mandates high-voltage safety training for any worker handling EV batteries (OSHA, 2025).

Can you put water on a lithium battery fire?

Yes, but you need a lot of it. NFPA guidelines recommend 3,000 to 8,000 gallons of water for sustained direct cooling of a lithium-ion battery fire (NFPA, 2024). Standard extinguishers won't cut it. Many fire departments now carry thermal imaging cameras to monitor battery cell temperatures for hours after the visible flames are gone. Plan your storage accordingly.

Are hybrid vehicles a good starting point for EV dismantling?

Hybrids are the best entry point, hands down. Their battery packs are smaller, lower voltage, and easier to handle than full BEV packs. You learn disconnect procedures, PPE habits, and storage protocols at lower risk. Most yards already have hybrids sitting on their lots right now. Start there before committing budget to full EV training and equipment.

---

EVs aren't replacing your business. They're adding a new layer to it. The core of what you do, pulling parts, pricing them fairly, and selling them to people who need them, doesn't change. But the parts themselves are evolving, and the safety requirements are serious.

The yards that start preparing now will be the ones selling $5,000 battery modules while their competitors are still searching "how to disconnect a Tesla battery pack" on YouTube. You've got 3-5 years of runway. That's enough time, but only if you actually use it.

Start with training. Practice on hybrids. Budget for equipment. And when the volume arrives, you'll be ready to handle it.

WhatsApp us: we're building EV-specific network rooms as volume grows and want to hear what you're seeing on your lot.

Every salvage vehicle you buy is a bet. You're betting the parts inside are worth more than what you paid, plus transport, plus the hours it takes to pull them. Get this math right consistently and your yard grows. Get it wrong and you're stacking steel that eats space and earns nothing.

Insurance companies totaled over 4.1 million vehicles in the US in 2023 (CCC Intelligent Solutions Crash Course, 2024). Supply isn't the problem. The challenge is picking the right vehicles, the ones where the profit math works before you ever raise your hand to bid. This guide covers where to source, what to look for, and the mistakes that drain your margins fastest.

Key Takeaways

  • Insurance companies totaled 4.1M+ US vehicles in 2023, creating steady supply for dismantlers (CCC Intelligent Solutions, 2024).
  • The 3-7 year vehicle age range balances strong parts demand against reasonable purchase prices.
  • Always calculate your bid ceiling before the auction, never during.
  • Copart and IAA dominate, but tow yard deals and insurance direct purchases offer less competition and lower costs.
  • A single $1,200 vehicle can yield $2,280 in parts, but only if you verify demand before you bid.

Where Should You Source Salvage Vehicles?

The two largest US salvage auction platforms, Copart and IAA (now part of RB Global), move millions of vehicles annually. Copart alone processed roughly 4 million vehicles in fiscal year 2024 (Copart 10-K Filing, 2024). But auctions aren't the only sourcing channel, and they're not always the best one for every vehicle type.

Online salvage auctions

Copart and IAA are where most dismantlers start. Both platforms list vehicles with photos, damage type, odometer readings, and run-and-drive status. You can bid from your desk, which saves a full day at the lot. Registration requires a state dealer or dismantler license in most jurisdictions.

The convenience comes with competition. Popular late-model vehicles attract dozens of bidders, and buyer's premiums add 10-18% on top of your winning bid. That overhead matters when you're calculating per-vehicle profit.

Insurance company direct deals

Some carriers sell totaled vehicles directly to licensed dismantlers, skipping the auction entirely. These deals carry lower prices because the insurer avoids auction listing fees. Building relationships with local adjusters and claims managers takes time. But once you're on their vendor list, you'll see vehicles before they reach the public platforms.

Tow yard relationships

Tow operators handle abandoned and unclaimed vehicles constantly. Many don't want the hassle of listing them at auction. A standing offer to buy abandoned vehicles at a flat rate creates a steady, low-cost supply line. The inventory skews older and less predictable, but the price often makes up for the risk.

Public auctions and estate sales

Municipal impound lots and estate liquidations occasionally surface vehicles most dismantlers overlook. Competition is lower than online platforms. Inventory quality varies, so treat these as a supplement to your primary channels, not a replacement.

Copart processed approximately 4 million vehicles in fiscal year 2024, according to its SEC 10-K filing. Online salvage auctions represent the largest sourcing channel for US dismantlers, but direct insurance deals and tow yard relationships can deliver lower per-vehicle costs through reduced competition and zero auction fees.

The Profit Math: A Worked Dismantling Example

A salvage buy only makes sense when the parts revenue outweighs total acquisition and labor costs. Net margins for salvage yards range from 10% to 20% of revenue (FinModelsLab, 2025). Better sourcing decisions push you toward the high end.

Here's a real example. You buy a 2019 Honda CR-V with front-end collision damage at Copart for $1,200.

Parts you can pull:
PartEstimated Revenue
Transmission$650
Motor$800
Headlight assemblies (pair)$180
Catalytic converter$250
Misc (mirrors, doors, electronics)$400
Total parts revenue$2,280
Subtract your purchase price ($1,200) and dismantling labor, roughly 4-6 hours at $350 all-in. That's $730 net profit from one vehicle.

That's the clean version. In practice, you also pay buyer's premium (18% on Copart, or $216), and transport runs $150-$500 depending on distance. On a $1,200 buy with $300 in transport and premium, your realistic net drops to $380-$500. Still solid. But it shows why the bid ceiling matters so much. Every dollar over your target eats directly into profit.

The key question before every bid: can you sell the parts fast enough to justify tying up the capital? A vehicle that sits six months waiting for buyers costs you in space, handling, and depreciation. Check demand first.

How Do You Evaluate a Vehicle Before Bidding?

Vehicles in the 3-7 year age range consistently yield the best dismantling returns. The average age of vehicles on US roads hit 12.6 years in 2024 (S&P Global Mobility, 2024), which means parts for 3-7 year old models carry strong demand from repair shops and retail buyers.

Damage pattern assessment

Not all damage is equal. Front-end collisions are often the best buys for dismantlers because the drivetrain, rear body, and interior typically survive intact. Rear-end damage can preserve the engine bay but destroy the trunk, tailgate, and sometimes the fuel system. Side impacts and rollovers tend to damage the most components across the vehicle, making yields unpredictable.

Over the years, we've found that front-end hits on late-model SUVs are the sweet spot. The bumper, grille, and hood are gone, but everything behind the firewall usually checks out. You lose maybe $300 in crushed body parts but keep $1,500 or more in drivetrain and electrical.

The mileage and year sweet spot

Vehicles under 80,000 miles with 3-7 years of age hit the demand curve perfectly. Parts from these vehicles are new enough that repair shops trust them and old enough that OEM replacements are expensive. Below 3 years, salvage prices run too high because clean-title buyers bid them up. Above 7 years, parts demand softens and prices drop.

Parts demand check

Before you bid on anything, check whether the parts you'll pull actually have buyers. Search Car-Part.com, which indexes over 200 million parts from yards nationwide (Car-Part.com, 2026). If twenty yards already list the same transmission, supply is high and your sale price drops. If only two or three list it, you've found a gap.

Bid ceiling discipline

Set your maximum bid before the auction starts. Write it down. Every dollar above that number comes directly out of your profit. The math doesn't care how much you wanted the vehicle.

Calculate your ceiling like this: estimated parts revenue minus labor minus transport minus fees minus your target profit. What's left is the most you can pay. If bidding pushes past that number, let it go. Another vehicle will come up tomorrow.

The average age of vehicles on US roads reached 12.6 years in 2024, according to S&P Global Mobility. For dismantlers, this aging fleet drives consistent demand for parts from 3-7 year old vehicles, which balance high parts value against reasonable auction prices.

Copart vs IAA: Which Platform Fits Dismantlers Better?

Copart and IAA (RB Global) together control the majority of US salvage vehicle auctions. Copart operates over 200 locations across North America (Copart.com, 2026). IAA runs a comparable network. Both serve dismantlers, but their fee structures and inventory mixes differ in ways that affect your bottom line.

Fee structures

Copart charges a buyer's premium that scales with the sale price. For basic members, expect roughly 18% on top of your winning bid. IAA's fee structure varies by membership tier, but licensed dealers and dismantlers often pay lower premiums in the 10-15% range. Both platforms charge additional gate fees, environmental fees, and title processing fees that add $50-$100 per vehicle.

Don't ignore these when calculating your bid ceiling. On a $1,500 vehicle, the difference between 18% and 12% buyer's premium is $90. Across 50 vehicles per year, that's $4,500 in savings.

Inventory differences

Copart tends to carry more insurance-consigned vehicles, including newer models and higher-value total losses. IAA's mix skews slightly toward older fleet vehicles and dealer trade-ins in some regions. Both platforms carry the full range, but checking both before each buy expands your options.

Bidding strategies that work

Don't bid early. On both platforms, early bids signal interest and attract competition. Place your bid in the final moments of the auction window. Set your ceiling, wait, and bid once. If you don't win, move on. There's no shortage of vehicles.

Use proxy bidding to set your maximum and let the system bid incrementally on your behalf. This prevents the emotional ratcheting that happens when you're watching a countdown timer.

Here's something most guides won't tell you: buy on rainy days and holiday weeks. Auction participation drops noticeably during bad weather and around holidays. The same vehicle that draws 15 bidders on a Tuesday in June might attract 6 on a Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Fewer bidders means lower prices.

What Mistakes Cost Salvage Buyers the Most Money?

The Automotive Recyclers Association estimates roughly 9,000 auto recycling businesses operate across the US (ARA, 2025). The ones that struggle with sourcing tend to make the same five mistakes repeatedly.

Bidding on emotion

You've been watching a 2021 Civic for three days. You've already imagined the parts on your shelves. The auction starts and someone outbids you by $50. So you bid again. And again. This is how a $1,200 buy becomes a $1,800 buy and your profit evaporates. The vehicle doesn't care how much time you spent researching it. Stick to your ceiling.

Ignoring transport costs

A vehicle listed 200 miles from your yard might look like a great deal until you add $400 in transport. Copart offers in-house shipping, but rates vary by distance and vehicle size (Copart.com, 2026). Always factor transport into your bid ceiling, not after you've won.

Skipping the demand check

Buying a vehicle because the price is low without checking whether anyone wants its parts is how yards end up with rows of unsaleable inventory. Check Car-Part.com and eBay sold listings before every bid. If supply already outweighs demand for the model's key parts, pass.

Overpaying for clean-title vehicles

Some dismantlers chase clean-title vehicles thinking they'll yield better parts. Sometimes that's true. But clean-title vehicles attract retail buyers who will always outbid you because they see a drivable car, not a parts donor. Focus on salvage-title and insurance total-loss vehicles where you're competing against other dismantlers, not retail shoppers.

Buying without a plan for the hull

After you pull the profitable parts, you've still got 2,500 pounds of steel. If you don't have a scrap buyer or a hull disposal arrangement, that weight sits on your lot eating space. Line up your scrap relationship before you start buying at volume.

Approximately 9,000 auto recycling businesses operate across the United States, according to the Automotive Recyclers Association. The most common sourcing mistake among these operations is emotional bidding, pushing past calculated bid ceilings chasing vehicles that looked good on screen but don't pencil out on paper.

How Do Demand Signals Improve Your Sourcing?

The smartest sourcing strategy isn't just finding cheap vehicles. It's buying vehicles that contain the parts people are actively requesting. Car-Part.com's index of over 200 million parts gives you supply data (Car-Part.com, 2026). But knowing what buyers want right now requires a different signal.

Listening to real-time requests

On voice parts networks like Hotline HQ, you hear live broadcasts from yards and shops requesting specific parts. Spend a week listening and patterns emerge. If you keep hearing requests for 2018-2022 Hyundai Tucson transmissions and nobody on the line has one, that's a buy signal. Next time a damaged Tucson shows up at auction, you know the demand is there before you bid.

That's the difference between speculative buying and informed buying. You're not guessing which parts will sell. You're responding to demand you've already heard.

Seasonal and regional patterns

Parts demand shifts with seasons and geography. AC compressors move in summer. Heater cores sell in winter. Body panels for popular trucks spike after hail season in the Midwest. If you track these patterns and time your auction purchases accordingly, you're buying into demand instead of hoping for it.

Car-Part.com indexes over 200 million parts from salvage yards nationwide, providing supply-side data for sourcing decisions. Combining this with real-time demand signals from voice parts networks and seasonal trends helps dismantlers buy vehicles that contain parts with verified, active buyer interest.

Vehicles 3-7 years old with front-end collision damage tend to yield the best returns. The drivetrain stays intact, which means you can pull the transmission, motor, and catalytic converter at full value. Honda, Toyota, and Hyundai models move fastest because parts demand stays consistently high across salvage networks (Car-Part.com, 2026).

Yes, but it takes relationship building. Some insurance carriers sell totaled vehicles directly to licensed dismantlers, bypassing auction fees. Contact local adjusters and claims managers. Once you're on their vendor list, you'll see vehicles before they reach Copart or IAA. Expect lower per-vehicle costs because the insurer skips auction listing fees and buyer premiums.

How much does it cost to get started buying at Copart?

Copart requires a state-issued dealer or dismantler license for direct bidding. Basic membership starts at around $200 per year. The main ongoing cost is the buyer's premium, roughly 18% on top of your winning bid (Copart.com, 2026). Factor in transport at $150-$500 per vehicle depending on distance, and you're looking at $350-$700 in per-vehicle overhead before you pull a single part.

Start Buying Smarter This Week

You don't need to overhaul your entire sourcing operation overnight. Start with two changes. First, calculate your bid ceiling for every vehicle before the auction opens, not during. Write the number on a notepad and don't go past it. Second, check parts demand on Car-Part.com before you bid on anything. Those two habits alone will filter out the bad buys that drain your margins.

This guide breaks down seven real options — what each one costs, how fast parts move, who's buying, and where each platform falls short. Whether you're clearing shelves at a yard or selling a transmission out of your garage, one of these fits.

*Disclosure: Hotline HQ publishes this guide and operates a voice hotline network (option 7 below). We've covered every platform honestly, including the trade-offs of our own.*

The 7 Best Places to Sell Used Auto Parts Online

The used auto parts market in the US generates an estimated $12 billion to $14 billion annually, with roughly 9,000 auto recycling businesses competing for buyers (Automotive Recyclers Association). That market supports a wide range of selling channels — from massive consumer marketplaces to specialized industry networks.

Here are the seven platforms that actually move used auto parts in 2026, ranked by the size of their buyer pool. Later, we'll break down which ones make sense for your specific situation.

For a broader look at how yards approach multi-channel selling, see our guide on how salvage yards sell more parts.

1. eBay Motors

Best for: Individual sellers and yards that want the widest consumer reach How it works: You create a listing with photos, part details, fitment data, and price. Buyers find your listing through eBay search or Google Shopping. When a part sells, you ship it or arrange local pickup. eBay handles payment processing.

eBay Motors is the 800-pound gorilla of online auto parts sales. The eBay marketplace overall sees roughly 133 million active buyers worldwide (eBay Inc., Q1 2025 earnings). The Parts & Accessories category is one of eBay's largest, and eBay Motors consistently ranks among the top results in Google for used auto parts searches.

Pricing and fees: eBay gives most sellers 250 free insertion listings per month. After that, insertion fees are typically $0.35 per listing. The final value fee runs approximately 14.35% of the total sale amount (including shipping), plus a $0.30 per-order surcharge. For a $200 transmission, you'd pay about $29 in fees after the sale closes. Speed of sale: Variable. High-demand parts from popular vehicles (Honda Civic headlights, F-150 tailgates) can sell within days. Niche parts for older or uncommon vehicles may sit for weeks or months. eBay works better as a long-tail play than a quick-sale channel. Reach: National and international. eBay's buyer pool is unmatched for consumer-facing parts sales. Buyers search by year, make, model, and part number — and eBay's fitment data system helps match your listing to the right vehicles. Pros:
  • Largest buyer pool of any platform
  • eBay's fitment tools help buyers find compatible parts
  • Built-in payment processing and buyer/seller protections
  • Strong Google Shopping and organic search visibility
  • Supports both auction and fixed-price formats
Cons:
  • Roughly 15% in fees on every sale eats into margins
  • Shipping logistics fall on you — heavy parts like engines and transmissions are expensive to ship
  • Returns and buyer disputes can be costly and time-consuming
  • Listing quality matters — poor photos and descriptions mean no sales
  • High competition from professional eBay parts sellers and large dismantlers

2. Facebook Marketplace

Best for: Local pickup sales with zero fees How it works: You post a listing with photos, description, and price. Buyers in your area browse or search Marketplace and message you directly. Transactions happen in person. There's no built-in payment processing for local sales — cash, Venmo, or Zelle are the norm.

Facebook Marketplace reaches an enormous audience. Meta reported over 3 billion monthly active users across its platforms in 2024, and Marketplace is available in most US markets. For auto parts, it works best when the buyer is within driving distance.

Pricing and fees: Zero fees for local pickup transactions. If you use Facebook's shipping option (available for some categories), a 10% selling fee applies with a $1.00 minimum. Most used auto parts transactions happen locally, so you'll typically pay nothing. Speed of sale: Fast for common, in-demand parts in populated areas. Slow or nonexistent in rural markets. Expect a lot of "Is this still available?" messages that go nowhere. Reach: Broad but local. Your listing is shown primarily to buyers within a radius you set (typically 40 to 100 miles). National reach is possible through shipping, but that defeats the main advantage of the platform. Pros:
  • No fees on local pickup sales
  • Huge local audience — almost everyone has a Facebook account
  • Easy to list from your phone with photos
  • Buyers can see your profile, which builds some trust
  • Works well for large, heavy parts that are impractical to ship
Cons:
  • No buyer verification or vetting — flaky buyers and no-shows are common
  • No fitment tools or structured parts data
  • Low-ball offers are relentless
  • No built-in payment protection for local sales
  • Listings expire and get buried quickly without re-posting
  • Not designed for auto parts — you're competing with furniture, electronics, and everything else

3. Car-Part.com

Best for: Salvage yards that want passive, always-on national exposure How it works: Yards running compatible inventory management software (especially Checkmate, which Car-Part.com owns) upload their inventory data to Car-Part.com's database. Buyers search by year, make, model, and part type. Results show which yards have the part, along with price and condition. The buyer then contacts the yard directly to arrange purchase and shipping.

Car-Part.com is the industry standard for used parts search. Over 200 million parts are searchable in their database (Car-Part.com). No other platform comes close in raw inventory size. If you run a salvage yard and you're not on Car-Part.com, you're invisible to a large chunk of the buying market.

Pricing and fees: Car-Part.com charges yards a subscription fee for listing access. Pricing varies by yard size and integration level but typically runs several hundred dollars per month. There are no per-sale commissions. For buyers, searching is free. Speed of sale: Passive. Parts sell when a buyer finds your listing and decides to call. You're not actively pushing parts — they sit in the database until someone searches for them. Speed depends on demand for the specific part and how many other yards have it listed. Reach: The largest in the used auto parts industry. The 200M+ parts database draws buyers ranging from repair shops and body shops to individual consumers doing their own repairs. For a deeper comparison of how Car-Part.com stacks up against other networks, see our platform comparison guide. Pros:
  • The largest used auto parts database in the industry
  • Standard tool that shops and buyers already know how to use
  • Passive exposure — parts sell without active effort once listed
  • No per-transaction fees
  • Integration with popular yard management software
Cons:
  • Inventory data freshness depends on how often you sync — a part sold yesterday might still show as available today
  • You need compatible inventory software to list effectively
  • Subscription costs regardless of how many parts you sell
  • Buyer contacts come in as phone calls or emails — no real-time push
  • High competition from other yards listing the same parts

For tips on setting yard pricing competitively across platforms, read our used auto parts pricing guide.

4. Craigslist

Best for: Free, no-frills local listings for heavy or hard-to-ship parts How it works: You post a classified ad with photos, a description, and your asking price. Buyers browse or search the auto parts section in their metro area. Communication happens through Craigslist's anonymized email relay or by phone number if you include one. All transactions are in person.

Craigslist has been around since 1995 and remains one of the most-visited classified sites in the US. For auto parts, it's a bare-bones option — no fitment data, no payment processing, no buyer verification.

Pricing and fees: Free. Craigslist charges nothing to post in the auto parts category in most markets. A few metro areas charge a small fee for certain categories, but parts and accessories listings are typically $0. Speed of sale: Unpredictable. You might sell a popular part the same day or re-post the same listing for months with no bites. Craigslist's audience for auto parts has shrunk as Facebook Marketplace and specialized platforms have gained ground. Reach: Local only. Each posting is tied to a specific metro area. There's no national search and no way to reach buyers outside your region. Pros:
  • Completely free
  • No account required (though one is available)
  • Simple to post — minimal barriers to listing
  • Works for large, heavy parts where local pickup is the only option
Cons:
  • Buyer quality is low — expect scam attempts, no-shows, and lowball offers
  • No structured data, fitment tools, or inventory integration
  • Listings get buried quickly and require frequent re-posting
  • No payment protection or dispute resolution
  • Declining traffic for auto parts compared to five years ago

  • Focus on the auto recycling industry rather than general commerce

  • Less name recognition — many shops haven't heard of PartCycle yet
  • Transaction fees still eat into margins, even if lower than eBay's
  • Requires inventory upload and platform onboarding
  • Not ideal for individual sellers — geared toward licensed yards

6. LKQ / Hollander

Best for: Yards already in the LKQ network or using Hollander interchange data How it works: LKQ Corporation is the largest buyer and reseller of recycled auto parts in North America. Hollander, which LKQ acquired, provides the interchange numbering system used across the industry to match parts across different vehicles. If you're an LKQ affiliate or supplier, parts move through their national distribution network. For independent yards, Hollander interchange numbers are essential for listing parts accurately on any platform.

LKQ operates over 800 locations across North America and generated roughly $14 billion in revenue in 2024 (LKQ Corporation, 2024 annual report). They sell to repair shops, insurance companies, and consumers. Independent yards can supply parts to LKQ as wholesale vendors.

Pricing and fees: If you sell to LKQ as a wholesale supplier, pricing is negotiated directly and typically at wholesale rates below what you'd get selling direct to shops or consumers. The trade-off is volume and speed — LKQ buys in quantity and pays reliably. Using Hollander interchange data for your own listings may involve a licensing fee depending on your yard management software. Speed of sale: Fast if you're selling wholesale to LKQ — they buy what they need and pay promptly. For parts moving through the broader LKQ retail network, speed depends on demand and location. Reach: The largest in the industry. LKQ's distribution network covers all major US markets and extends into Europe. The Hollander interchange system is the standard reference for parts interchangeability across the entire recycling industry. Pros:
  • Access to the largest auto parts distribution network in North America
  • Reliable wholesale buyer if you become an LKQ supplier
  • Hollander interchange numbers are the industry standard for parts identification
  • Volume purchasing means faster inventory turnover
  • LKQ handles logistics, distribution, and customer service on their end
Cons:
  • Wholesale pricing means lower per-part margins
  • LKQ competes with independent yards for the same buyers
  • Supplying LKQ means you're helping a competitor grow
  • Hollander data licensing costs can add up for smaller operations
  • Less control over pricing and customer relationships
  • Not a platform you "list on" — it's a supply relationship

7. Hotline HQ

Best for: Salvage yards that want the fastest yard-to-yard sales channel How it works: Hotline HQ connects over 500 salvage yards across 12 regional conference rooms on a live voice network. Your yard's desk phone stays connected to your regional room — California, Texas, Florida, Arizona, and others. When any yard on the network needs a part, they key up and describe it: "2019 Ram 1500 left headlight assembly." Every connected yard hears the request in real time. You have the part? Key up, respond, and close the deal directly. Average response time: approximately 2 seconds (Hotline HQ network data).

No database. No inventory upload. No waiting for someone to find your listing. Live voice, live response.

Pricing and fees: Flat monthly membership fee. No per-call charges, no listing fees, no per-sale commission. A preconfigured desk phone ships with your membership. For current pricing, see HotlineHQ.com. Speed of sale: The fastest of any channel covered in this guide. A broadcast goes out, every yard in the room hears it, and responses come back in seconds. There's no listing-and-wait cycle. Parts that would sit in a database for weeks move the same day on the hotline because someone, somewhere on the network, needs it right now. Reach: Over 500 yards across major US markets. Reach is regional — you hear broadcasts from yards in your room and nearby rooms. It's not a national consumer marketplace, and it doesn't replace platforms that reach individual buyers. It supplements them with a fast, direct, yard-to-yard channel.

For a full breakdown of how the network operates, see our guide on how auto parts hotlines work. For a side-by-side look at how Hotline HQ compares to other industry networks, read PartsHotlines vs. Car-Part.com vs. Hotline HQ.

Pros:
  • Fastest time-to-sale of any channel — seconds, not days
  • One broadcast reaches 100+ yards simultaneously
  • Flat monthly fee with no commissions or per-sale costs
  • No inventory upload or database management required
  • Built for the way yards already work — voice, not clicks
  • Direct yard-to-yard relationships with no middleman
Cons:
  • Yard-to-yard only — doesn't reach individual consumers
  • Regional model means coverage varies by market
  • Requires a desk phone and someone at the counter to respond
  • Not a fit for individual sellers or one-off part sales
  • Newer network — smaller than Car-Part.com's 200M+ parts database

Which Platform Fits Your Operation

Seven platforms, seven different strengths. Here's the short version of which one fits whom:

You're a salvage yard or dismantler moving volume: Start with Car-Part.com for passive national reach and Hotline HQ for fast yard-to-yard sales. These two cover different needs and complement each other well. Add eBay Motors if you have the staff to manage listings and ship parts to individual buyers. You're a small yard with limited staff: Hotline HQ requires the least overhead — no inventory uploads, no listing management, just listen and respond. Car-Part.com adds passive exposure if your yard management software supports it. You're an individual selling a few parts: eBay Motors gives you the widest audience. Facebook Marketplace works for local pickup of large parts. Craigslist is free but slower and riskier. You want the lowest fees possible: Facebook Marketplace (free for local) and Craigslist (free) cost nothing. Hotline HQ's flat fee means no per-sale hit. eBay's roughly 15% fee is the most expensive option. You want the fastest sale: Hotline HQ. Nothing else in this industry matches a 2-second response on a live voice broadcast. Everything else — eBay, Facebook, Car-Part.com — involves waiting for someone to find your listing and decide to reach out.

To understand how pricing affects which channel works best for different parts, check our used auto parts pricing guide. For data on which parts generate the most demand across these platforms, see the most-requested used auto parts.

Why One Channel Isn't Enough

The yards that consistently move the most inventory don't rely on a single platform. They stack channels. A typical high-volume yard might run Car-Part.com for passive database exposure, Hotline HQ for real-time yard-to-yard sales, and eBay Motors for direct-to-consumer sales on high-margin parts.

Each channel solves a different problem. Car-Part.com catches buyers who search. Hotline HQ catches buyers who broadcast. eBay catches consumers who Google. Facebook catches locals who browse.

The risk of relying on one channel is obvious: if eBay raises fees, if Car-Part.com's data gets stale, if Facebook changes its algorithm, your sales drop overnight. Two or three channels give you redundancy and reach different buyer types.

Start with the channel that matches how your operation already works. If you have good inventory data, add Car-Part.com. If you have a counter person who can respond quickly, add Hotline HQ. If you have someone who can photograph and list parts, add eBay. Then expand from there.

Self-service yards (also called u-pull-it or pick-a-part) let you remove parts yourself. Full-service yards pull, test, and sometimes warranty the part for you.

Roughly 9,000 auto recycling facilities operate across the United States, according to the Automotive Recyclers Association (ARA, 2024). No single search method reaches all of them, so your best move is knowing which tool to reach for depending on what you need.

Google Maps and Local Search

The quickest way to find a salvage yard near you is to open Google Maps and search "junkyard near me," "salvage yard near me," or "used auto parts near me." Google pulls up a map with pins, ratings, phone numbers, hours, and directions.

This works well for getting oriented. You'll see which yards are closest, which ones have decent reviews, and which ones are open right now. For common parts on common vehicles, this might be all you need. Pick the closest yard with 4+ stars, call ahead, and drive over.

Where Google Maps falls short is coverage. Smaller yards, especially rural operations, often don't have a Google Business Profile or rank poorly in local search. A yard 15 miles away with exactly the part you need might not show up because a bigger operation closer to you dominates the results.

Also, Google won't tell you whether a specific yard has your part. It tells you the yard exists. You still need to call.

Tips for better local search results

  • Search for the specific part type: "used transmission shop near me" or "salvage engines near me" sometimes surfaces specialty yards
  • Expand the map radius manually by zooming out, then browsing pins outside your immediate area
  • Check Google reviews for mentions of the vehicle make you need -- reviewers often mention specific brands a yard specializes in

Why does the association listing matter? Because a yard that pays dues and submits to inspections is more likely to operate professionally, price fairly, and honor a return. That's not a guarantee. But it filters out fly-by-night operations that buy wrecks, strip the easy parts, and leave you with no recourse if something is wrong.

It's designed for speed and for parts that are hard to find through traditional search. Where databases show you what was in stock last time someone updated a listing, a voice broadcast confirms what's actually available right now.

This method works best when you need a part fast, when you're looking for something uncommon, or when you've already struck out on Car-Part.com and want a real-time check across multiple yards. For a deeper look at how voice-based parts sourcing works, read our guide on how auto parts hotlines work.

If you're an individual car owner rather than a yard, Hotline HQ is primarily a yard-to-yard network. But you can ask your local repair shop or salvage yard if they're on the network and can broadcast a request on your behalf.

Craigslist, Facebook Groups, and Forums

Free options exist, and they work -- sometimes. Craigslist auto parts listings show what's available in your immediate area. Facebook Marketplace and local auto parts groups can surface deals from people parting out vehicles in their driveways. Car-specific forums (model-year forums, enthusiast boards) are especially useful for older or specialty vehicles where salvage yard coverage is thin.

The downside is time. You're scrolling through unstructured listings with inconsistent descriptions, no standardized pricing, and no warranty. Scam listings appear regularly on all three platforms. There is no way to search 50 yards at once the way you can with Car-Part.com or a voice network.

When Craigslist and Facebook groups are worth your time:

  • You're looking for a cheap, common part and you're not in a rush
  • You need a part for an older or specialty vehicle (pre-1990, import, performance car) that salvage yards may have already crushed
  • You're parting out your own vehicle and want to see local pricing before you list
  • You live in a rural area with few salvage yards within driving distance

When they're not worth the effort:

  • You need the part today or tomorrow
  • You need a verified, warrantied component
  • You're sourcing for a shop and need consistent supply

Self-Service vs Full-Service Yards

Salvage yards fall into two broad categories, and knowing the difference before you visit saves time and frustration.

Self-service yards (u-pull-it / pick-a-part)

You walk the lot, find the vehicle, and remove the part yourself. Pricing is standardized -- most self-service yards use a fixed price list based on part type, not vehicle make or model. An alternator costs the same whether it came off a Civic or a Camry.

Self-service yards charge the lowest prices in the industry. Expect to pay 50 to 70 percent less than retail salvage prices. The trade-off is labor: you need your own tools, you need to know how to remove the part without breaking it, and the experience can be physically demanding, especially in summer heat or winter cold.

Major self-service chains include LKQ Pick Your Part, Pull-A-Part, and Ecology Auto Parts. Most metro areas have at least one independent u-pull-it yard as well.

Full-service yards

The yard pulls the part for you. They typically test it, clean it, and offer a warranty (30 to 90 days is standard). You tell them what you need, they check inventory, pull it, and you pick it up or they ship it. Prices are higher than self-service, but you're paying for labor, testing, and a return policy.

Full-service yards are the better choice when:

  • You don't have tools or mechanical experience
  • You need an engine, transmission, or another component that's difficult to remove
  • You want a warranty and the ability to return the part if it's defective
  • You're buying for a customer's vehicle and can't afford to install a bad part

Which type is near you?

Search for "u-pull-it near me" or "pick-a-part near me" for self-service. Search for "auto recycler near me" or "used auto parts dealer near me" for full-service. Many cities have both types within reasonable driving distance.

What to Bring and What to Ask

Visiting a salvage yard without preparation wastes your time. Here's what experienced yard shoppers bring and ask.

What to bring

  • Your own tools. Self-service yards require them. Even at full-service yards, having a socket set in the truck lets you verify fitment on the spot.
  • Year, make, model, and trim level. Write it down or keep it on your phone. A 2014 Accord EX and a 2014 Accord LX use different parts in some cases.
  • The old part, if possible. Bring the broken one so you can compare side by side. Connector shapes, bolt patterns, and mounting points vary between model years.
  • Gloves and closed-toe shoes. Yards are full of sharp metal, broken glass, and fluids. Most self-service yards require closed-toe shoes for entry.
  • Cash. Some smaller yards still prefer cash and may offer a discount for it. All yards accept cards, but asking about a cash price is worth the question.

What to ask

  • "Do you have a warranty or return policy?" Get the terms in writing or at least confirmed verbally before you pay.
  • "Is this the original part or a replacement?" Rebuilt or aftermarket parts sometimes end up in salvage vehicles. You want to know what you're getting.
  • "Can you look up the interchange number?" Full-service yards with Hollander or Car-Part interchange data can tell you which other vehicles use the same part, expanding your options.
  • "Do you deliver or ship?" Many full-service yards ship parts regionally for a flat fee. If the closest yard with your part is two hours away, shipping may be cheaper than the drive.

How to negotiate

Salvage yard pricing is more flexible than most people assume. Here's what works:

  • Buying multiple parts from the same yard gives you leverage. Ask for a package discount.
  • Parts that have been sitting on the shelf for months are negotiable. If a part looks dusty, ask.
  • Cash discounts are common at independent yards. Ask, "Is there a cash price?"
  • If you find the same part listed cheaper on Car-Part.com at another yard, mention it. Many yards will match or beat a competitor's price to avoid losing the sale.

When to Go Local vs Online

The right answer depends on what you need and how fast you need it.

Go local when:
  • The part is common and readily available (headlights, mirrors, door handles, body panels for popular vehicles)
  • You want to inspect the part before buying
  • You need the part today and can't wait for shipping
  • You're comfortable removing the part yourself and want the lowest possible price
  • The part is large or heavy, making shipping costs prohibitive (hoods, doors, bumper assemblies)
Search online when:
  • The part is uncommon, discontinued, or for an older vehicle
  • No local yard has the vehicle in stock
  • You want to compare prices across multiple yards and regions
  • You need the part shipped to a repair shop or your home
  • You're looking for a specific trim-level or option-package variant

Many searches start local and go online when the local yards come up empty. That's normal. Start with the yard 10 minutes away. If they don't have it, search Car-Part.com. If that doesn't produce a result, try a voice broadcast through Hotline HQ or browse the methods in our online parts-finding guide.

For pricing benchmarks before you buy, our used auto parts pricing guide covers what to expect across common part categories.

Salvage Yard Hotspots by Region

Not all states are created equal when it comes to used parts availability. Vehicle registrations, climate, accident rates, and the age of the vehicle fleet all affect how many yards operate and what they stock.

California

The largest market for used auto parts in the US. California has over 800 licensed auto dismantlers, concentrated in the Los Angeles basin, the Inland Empire, and the Central Valley. The mild climate means less rust, which makes California yards a go-to source for body panels and structural parts shipped nationwide. Strict environmental regulations mean California yards tend to be well-run and compliant. See our full California used auto parts page.

Texas

Texas ranks second in the number of salvage yards, with heavy concentration in Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth, San Antonio, and the Rio Grande Valley. The Texas market specializes in trucks and SUVs -- Ford F-150 parts, Chevy Silverado parts, and Ram parts are always in stock somewhere. Hail damage in North Texas feeds a steady supply of late-model vehicles into the recycling pipeline. Our Texas page has more detail.

Florida

Florida's high accident rate and year-round driving season keep a large number of late-model vehicles flowing into salvage. The state has strong representation in yards carrying imports, especially Toyota, Honda, and Nissan. Coastal yards may have salt-air corrosion on some parts, so inspect carefully. Check our Florida page.

Arizona

Arizona is known for rust-free parts. The desert climate preserves body panels, undercarriages, and trim pieces in ways that yards in the Midwest and Northeast can't match. Arizona yards are a popular source for restoration projects and out-of-state buyers who need clean sheet metal. Many Arizona yards ship nationally. See our Arizona page.

Other notable regions

The Midwest (Ohio, Michigan, Indiana) has a high density of yards but rust is a significant factor on body parts. The Pacific Northwest (Oregon, Washington) feeds a steady supply of Subaru and Japanese import parts. The Northeast corridor (New Jersey, Pennsylvania, New York) has tight environmental regulations and high competition, which keeps pricing competitive.

Find the Part, Not Just the Yard

Knowing where the yards are is step one. Getting the actual part into your hands is step two, and the gap between those two steps is where most people lose time and money.

If you're searching for something specific, don't limit yourself to one method. Search Google Maps for what's close. Search Car-Part.com for what's in stock. Check your state recycler association for yards you haven't tried. And if you're still coming up empty, try a live voice broadcast through a network like Hotline HQ to reach yards that might have the part but didn't list it in any database.

The used auto parts market is big -- over $15 billion annually in the US, according to IBIS World (2025). The part you need almost certainly exists somewhere. The question is how quickly you can find it and at what price. Use the right tools, call ahead, and don't drive to a yard without confirming they have the vehicle in stock.
