posts.bodyHtml:
Disclosure: Hotline HQ publishes this guide. We operate a voice parts network used by 500+ salvage yards. We'll mention our product once, where it's relevant, and flag it. Every software recommendation below stands on its own.

The average US salvage yard stocks around 3,000 saleable parts at any given time. Without software, you're tracking those parts on paper, in spreadsheets, or in your head. That worked 20 years ago. It doesn't work now that buyers expect instant answers and online listings.

The Automotive Recyclers Association reports that roughly 78% of active US yards now use some form of digital inventory management (ARA, 2025). That number was closer to 50% a decade ago. The shift isn't hype. It's survival. Yards that can't tell a caller whether they have a 2019 Camry transmission in stock lose that sale to a yard that can answer in five seconds.

This guide compares seven salvage yard software tools that dismantlers actually use. I've included what each does, who it fits, and what it costs. No fluff, no rankings designed to push you toward the most expensive option. If you're building a broader growth strategy, this fits alongside our pillar guide on growing a salvage yard business.

Key Takeaways

  • Seven tools dominate the salvage yard software market. Each fits a different yard size, budget, and sales channel.
  • 78% of US yards now use digital inventory, up from roughly 50% a decade ago (ARA, 2025).
  • Software tracks your stock. A voice network finds buyers. Most successful yards run both.
  • Hollander interchange data underpins nearly every serious tool. If yours doesn't have it, you're pricing blind.

Why Does Salvage Yard Software Matter in 2026?

The US vehicle recycling market hit $85.5 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $165 billion by 2033, according to Verified Market Research (2024). That kind of growth attracts competition. Software is the baseline that separates yards that scale from yards that stall.

Good salvage yard software handles five core jobs: vehicle acquisition, parts cataloging, interchange lookup, pricing, and sales tracking. Some tools add marketplace syndication, accounting, or fleet management on top.

But here's what matters most. Interchange data. The Hollander interchange system maps which parts fit across makes, models, and years. When a customer asks for a 2017 Ford F-150 headlight, the interchange tells you whether the 2018 or 2019 version is the same part. Without it, you're guessing, and guessing costs sales.

We've talked to hundreds of yard owners through our network, and the pattern is consistent: yards that adopt structured inventory software within their first two years of operation report fewer lost sales and faster part lookups than yards that wait. The ones who wait often describe the transition as "painful but worth it."

Every tool below addresses these core jobs differently. The right pick depends on your yard's size, your primary sales channels, and how much you're willing to spend. Let's walk through each one.

Hollander/Pinnacle

Hollander has been the backbone of salvage yard data since the 1930s. Their interchange numbering system is the industry standard. Pinnacle is Hollander's full yard management platform, and it's the most established name in this space.

How it works

Pinnacle runs the entire dismantling workflow, from vehicle check-in through parts sales. You scan a VIN, and the system pulls interchange data, identifies saleable parts, and generates pull lists. It integrates directly with Hollander's proprietary interchange database, the same database that most other tools license or reference.

Pinnacle also handles yard mapping, warranty tracking, and core management. For yards that need to report to state agencies or manage environmental compliance, the reporting tools cover that too.

Best for

Large, established yards that want a proven, full-featured platform. Multi-location operations benefit from Pinnacle's centralized data architecture. If you've been in business for more than a decade, there's a good chance you've already encountered Hollander's interchange numbers.

Pricing

Quote-based. Pricing depends on yard size, user count, and modules. Expect enterprise-level pricing. Hollander doesn't publish rates, and implementation costs can be significant because the system is comprehensive.

Citation capsule: Hollander's interchange numbering system, introduced in the 1930s, remains the de facto standard for cross-referencing auto parts across makes, models, and years. Pinnacle, Hollander's yard management platform, integrates this interchange data directly into the dismantling workflow, making it the most data-rich option for large salvage operations (Hollander, 2025).

Dismantly

Dismantly is one of the newer names in salvage yard software. It launched with a cloud-first approach and leans heavily on AI-assisted part identification. If your yard sells through eBay, Facebook Marketplace, or other online channels, this one's worth a close look.

How it works

You photograph a vehicle or part, and Dismantly's system suggests what to pull based on current market demand. It generates listings and syndicates them across multiple marketplaces from one dashboard. Update a price or mark a part as sold, and the change pushes everywhere.

Inspection checklists help standardize how your team grades parts, which matters when you've got three different people pulling inventory and each one has a different idea of what "good condition" means.

Best for

Small to mid-size yards that sell heavily online. If you're listing 50 or more parts per week on eBay and Facebook, Dismantly's multi-channel sync saves real hours.

Pricing

Monthly subscription, tiered by inventory volume and marketplace integrations. Generally mid-range. Expect $100 to $300 per month depending on your plan.

I've seen yards cut their listing time in half after switching to a tool like Dismantly. The AI cataloging isn't perfect, it sometimes misidentifies trim levels, but it's faster than manual data entry for 90% of common parts.

Citation capsule: Dismantly uses AI-assisted part identification and multi-channel marketplace syndication to help salvage yards list parts across eBay, Facebook Marketplace, and other platforms from a single dashboard. Its cloud-based architecture provides mobile access, making it particularly suited for yards with fewer than 500 vehicles that prioritize online sales (Dismantly, 2026).

YardSmart

YardSmart targets the multi-yard operator. If you're running two, three, or five locations, the challenge isn't just tracking parts. It's knowing which yard has the part a customer needs right now.

How it works

YardSmart integrates Hollander interchange data and tracks inventory across multiple locations with a centralized view. It handles yard-to-yard transfers, so when Location A gets a request for a part that's sitting at Location B, the system shows it immediately.

Reporting is YardSmart's other strength. You can break down which vehicles and parts generate the most revenue, by location, by month, by category. That data feeds smarter buying decisions at auction.

Best for

Multi-location operations. If you're running a single yard with under 300 vehicles, YardSmart is more tool than you need. But if you've got two or more lots, the centralized inventory view pays for itself quickly.

Pricing

Quote-based. Pricing scales with yard count, user seats, and modules. Expect it to climb fast once you start adding locations and features.

Citation capsule: YardSmart provides multi-yard inventory management with Hollander interchange integration, enabling centralized part tracking and yard-to-yard transfers. It is primarily designed for salvage operations running two or more locations that need consolidated reporting across all sites (YardSmart, 2026).

Car-Part Checkmate

Car-Part.com is the largest used auto parts search engine in the US, indexing over 200 million parts from thousands of yards (Car-Part.com, 2025). Checkmate is their inventory management tool, and its biggest advantage is obvious: it feeds your parts directly into that massive search network.

How it works

Checkmate manages your yard's inventory and pushes it straight to Car-Part.com's buyer network. When a shop or DIY customer searches Car-Part.com for a 2016 Honda Civic alternator, your inventory shows up if you've got one. No separate listing step. Interchange data is built in, sourced from Car-Part.com's own extensive database.

The system also handles core tracking, customer management, and basic reporting. It's not trying to be a full business management suite. It's trying to connect your parts with the largest pool of buyers searching for them.

Best for

Yards where the majority of remote sales come through Car-Part.com searches. If you already get 40% or more of your phone calls from Car-Part.com listings, Checkmate tightens that pipeline significantly.

Pricing

Subscription-based, often bundled with Car-Part.com listing fees. Mid-range, similar to Dismantly. The bundled model can be cost-effective if Car-Part.com is your primary channel.

Citation capsule: Car-Part Checkmate provides native integration with Car-Part.com's 200-million-part search network. Yards using Checkmate push inventory updates directly to where millions of monthly buyer searches happen, eliminating the delay between cataloging a part and making it visible to buyers (Car-Part.com, 2025).

Frazer DMS

Frazer has been building dealer management software for decades. Their DMS covers the full business cycle, from buying vehicles at auction to selling parts to closing the books at year end. It's the old guard, and it's still standing for a reason.

How it works

Frazer runs on desktop, not the cloud. You install it locally, and it handles vehicle acquisition, dismantling workflows, parts inventory, sales, and, this is the big differentiator, integrated accounting. If you're running QuickBooks alongside your inventory system and manually reconciling between them, Frazer eliminates that step.

Title management is built in, too. For yards that buy vehicles at auction, having acquisition paperwork, title processing, and inventory all in one system reduces the paperwork shuffle.

Best for

Yards that want one system for everything, especially those that also buy and sell whole vehicles alongside parts. If your accountant is tired of importing data from two different programs, Frazer's integrated books are the selling point.

Pricing

Quote-based with licensing fees. Desktop installation means no monthly cloud subscription, but you'll pay for updates and support. Implementation costs vary.

Citation capsule: Frazer DMS is a desktop-based dealer management system covering the complete salvage yard business cycle, including vehicle acquisition, parts inventory, sales, and integrated accounting. Its decades-long track record makes it the most established all-in-one option for yards that want financial reporting and inventory management in a single installed system (Frazer Computing, 2026).

CRUSH (IAA)

CRUSH is IAA's (Insurance Auto Auctions) yard management platform. If you're already buying vehicles through IAA auctions, CRUSH ties your acquisition pipeline directly into your dismantling and inventory workflow.

How it works

CRUSH connects to IAA's auction platform, so vehicles you buy flow automatically into your yard management system. From there, it handles dismantling schedules, parts inventory, and sales tracking. The integration with IAA's auction data means you can track acquisition costs per vehicle and measure actual ROI on each car you dismantle.

The system also supports environmental compliance reporting, which matters in states with strict regulations around fluid disposal and hazardous materials.

Best for

Yards that source heavily from IAA auctions. If 50% or more of your vehicles come through IAA, the seamless auction-to-yard pipeline eliminates manual data entry from that process. Also useful for yards in states with strict environmental compliance requirements.

Pricing

Quote-based. Pricing typically connects to your IAA buyer relationship. Contact IAA directly for current rates.

CRUSH is often overlooked in software comparisons because it's tied to an auction house rather than positioned as standalone yard software. But for yards that already buy through IAA, the acquisition-to-inventory automation is genuinely valuable, possibly the strongest single integration on this list for that specific workflow.

Citation capsule: CRUSH, operated by IAA (Insurance Auto Auctions), integrates the vehicle acquisition pipeline directly with yard management. Vehicles purchased at IAA auctions flow into inventory automatically, enabling yards to track per-vehicle acquisition costs and dismantling ROI without manual data re-entry (IAA, 2026).

Yard Manager

Yard Manager is the budget option, and I don't mean that as an insult. Not every yard needs enterprise software. If you're moving from spreadsheets to your first real system, Yard Manager covers the basics without the sticker shock.

How it works

Parts tracking, pull lists, dismantle lists, and basic inventory search. That's the core. You log vehicles, track which parts have been pulled, schedule what's next for dismantling, and look up what's in stock when a customer calls.

It doesn't do marketplace syndication. It doesn't have deep interchange data. It doesn't handle accounting. What it does, it does simply, and for a lot of small yards, that's enough.

Best for

Smaller yards with under 200 vehicles that need structured inventory tracking at a low cost. A solid stepping stone for yards that plan to upgrade to a more feature-rich platform later.

Pricing

The most budget-friendly option in this comparison. Subscription or license model, typically under $100 per month. Some plans run even lower depending on feature tier.

Citation capsule: Yard Manager provides foundational inventory management, including parts tracking, pull lists, and dismantle scheduling, at the lowest price point among major salvage yard software tools. It is best suited for single-location yards with fewer than 200 vehicles transitioning from spreadsheets to structured software (SalvageSoftware, 2026).

Here's how all seven tools stack up across the features that matter most.

How Do You Choose the Right Junkyard Management Tool?

According to the IBISWorld Auto Parts Recycling industry report (2025), the average US salvage yard generates around $1.2 million in annual revenue. Your software should match the scale and complexity of that revenue, not exceed it.

Three factors should drive your decision.

Your primary sales channel. If you sell 60% of your parts through online marketplaces, Dismantly's multi-channel sync is worth the subscription. If Car-Part.com drives most of your remote inquiries, Checkmate's native integration is hard to beat. If you sell mostly to walk-ins and phone callers, you don't need marketplace features at all. Your yard count. Single yard under 300 vehicles? Start with Yard Manager or Dismantly and upgrade when you outgrow them. Multiple locations? YardSmart or Hollander/Pinnacle from day one. The cost of running disconnected systems across multiple lots adds up faster than you'd expect. Your budget. Yard Manager gets you in the door for under $100 per month. Dismantly and Checkmate sit in the mid-range. YardSmart, Frazer, Hollander/Pinnacle, and CRUSH cost more but cover more ground. Match the investment to your revenue, not your ambition. You can always upgrade.

What about interchange data? If the tool you're evaluating doesn't include Hollander or equivalent interchange lookup, think twice. Interchange is how you turn one part number into five compatible listings across model years. Without it, you're leaving sales on the table.

Software Manages Inventory, a Hotline Finds Buyers

Every tool in this comparison solves the same fundamental problem: knowing what's on your lot. That's table stakes. You can't run a serious yard without it. But inventory software doesn't generate demand. It organizes your supply.

Here's the gap. A buyer has to find your listing, click on it, and call you. That works for high-demand parts. But what about the 2014 Chevy Cruze rear bumper that's been sitting in your warehouse for three months? No one's searching for it. Your listing data goes stale between updates. The part collects dust.

A voice-based parts network works the other side. A yard broadcasts a parts request to every connected yard in the region. If you've got it, you respond in seconds. No listing required. No waiting for a search algorithm to surface your part. The average broadcast-to-response time on live voice networks is under 5 seconds, fast enough to close a deal before the caller moves on.

We've watched yards run Checkmate or Dismantly for inventory and use a voice network to move the parts that listings alone never sold. The software tracks what you have. The hotline puts a buyer's voice in your ear asking for exactly that part. They're not competing tools. They're complementary.

The yards moving the most parts in 2026 are stacking channels: walk-in traffic, online marketplaces, Car-Part.com listings, and live voice networks. No single tool covers all of that. The smart play is to pick the inventory software that fits your yard, then add demand-generation tools on top. If you want to understand how channel stacking works in practice, our guide to selling more parts breaks it down.

If you're ready to add a live demand channel alongside your software, sign up free and hear buyer requests hitting the network within minutes.

FAQ

What is the best salvage yard software for a small yard?

For a yard with under 500 vehicles, Yard Manager or Dismantly offer the lowest barrier to entry. Yard Manager covers the basics, pull lists and dismantle scheduling, at the lowest monthly cost. Dismantly adds AI-assisted cataloging and marketplace sync if you sell online. Both beat spreadsheets on day one.

Does salvage yard software replace a parts hotline?

No. They solve different problems. Software tracks what's on your lot. A voice hotline broadcasts live buyer requests to hundreds of yards simultaneously. Most yards run both. Software organizes your supply, and the hotline surfaces demand you'd never see from a listing alone. For more on how networking works, read our guide to yard-to-yard networking.

How much does auto dismantler inventory software cost?

Pricing ranges widely. Yard Manager starts under $100 per month. Cloud tools like Dismantly and Checkmate run $100 to $300 per month depending on features. YardSmart, Frazer, Hollander/Pinnacle, and CRUSH use quote-based pricing that scales with yard count and modules. Most vendors require a demo before quoting.

What is the Hollander interchange system, and why does it matter?

The Hollander interchange system maps which parts are compatible across different makes, models, and years. It's been the industry standard since the 1930s. When a customer asks for a part from a 2017 F-150, interchange data tells you whether the 2016 or 2018 version fits. Without it, you lose cross-reference sales. Most serious salvage yard software includes Hollander data or an equivalent.

Can I switch salvage yard software without losing my inventory data?

Yes, but expect a migration effort. Most vendors offer data import tools or migration assistance. The pain depends on how clean your current data is. Yards moving from spreadsheets to structured software often spend a week or two on data cleanup. Yards switching between established platforms can usually export and import with vendor support. Ask about migration before you commit to any tool. The cost of switching later is real, which is why buying the right vehicles upfront and tracking them properly from day one matters.

Most salvage yards don't market. They rely on word of mouth, a sign on the road, and whatever reputation they've built over the years. That worked for a long time. It's not enough anymore.

Here's why: 81% of auto parts buyers start their search online (PYP Accelerator, 2025). If your yard doesn't show up when someone searches "used transmission near me," you're invisible to that buyer. They'll find a yard that does show up.

The good news? Salvage yard marketing doesn't require a big budget or a marketing degree. The channels with the highest impact are free or close to it. This playbook ranks six marketing approaches by effort and return. It's part of a broader strategy for growing your salvage yard business.

Why Does Salvage Yard Marketing Start With Google?

An optimized Google Business Profile can lift walk-in traffic by 30-50% for salvage yards (PYP Accelerator, 2025). It costs nothing. It takes about 15 minutes a week to maintain. And it's the first thing potential customers see when they search for auto parts in your area. Most yards have a listing. Very few have optimized it.

Upload Real Photos, Not Stock

Google rewards listings with photos. Upload at least 20 pictures of your actual yard: the lot, the office, shelves with labeled parts, your crew at work. Forget stock images. Buyers can spot them, and so can Google's algorithm.

Take fresh photos every month or two. Updated images signal to Google that your business is active. They also give repeat visitors a reason to click on your listing again.

We've seen yards add 25 photos over a single weekend and notice more direction requests within two weeks. It's one of those rare tasks that takes an hour and keeps paying off for months.

Respond to Every Review Within 24 Hours

87% of consumers read online reviews when evaluating local businesses (BrightLocal, 2023). That stat applies to your junkyard Google Business Profile just like it applies to restaurants and plumbers. When someone searches "salvage yard near me," reviews are the first thing they scan after your name.

Respond to every review. Thank the five-star ones briefly. Address the one-star complaints honestly, and don't get defensive. A thoughtful response to a bad review builds more trust than ten good reviews with no owner replies.

Ask satisfied customers for reviews at the counter. Keep it simple: "If you've got a minute, a Google review really helps us out." Most people will if you ask.

Google also uses review volume and rating quality as a local ranking signal. More reviews with higher ratings push your listing above competitors in the map pack. It's not just reputation. It's search visibility.

Google Business Profile lets you publish short posts. Use them. Share new inventory arrivals, parts you just pulled, or vehicles you brought in. Mention specific makes and models. Those details help with salvage yard SEO.

NAP means Name, Address, Phone number. These three details must match everywhere your business appears online: Google, Yelp, Facebook, your website, every directory listing. Website Basics That Actually Drive Parts Sales

46% of all Google searches have local intent (HubSpot, 2024). That means nearly half the people searching right now want something nearby, including used auto parts. Phone Number Above the Fold

Your phone number should be the first thing visitors see. Not buried in a contact page. Not hidden in the footer. Put it at the top of every page, big enough to tap on a phone screen. One tap should start a call.

Most auto parts buyers who find your site want to call and ask about a specific part. Make calling as easy as possible. Remove every obstacle between the visitor and that phone call.

Make sure your site loads fast on mobile too. Over half of auto parts searches happen on phones. A slow, cluttered site loses visitors before they ever see your inventory or your number.

Build Make-and-Model Pages

Create individual pages for the makes and models you stock. "Used Honda Parts in Dallas." "Toyota Camry Transmission in Phoenix." These pages rank well in local search because almost no other yards bother to create them.

Each page doesn't need a thousand words. List the makes you typically carry, mention your city, include your phone number, and add a few photos of real parts. That's enough to outrank most local competitors who don't have these pages at all.

For broader reach, list your parts on Car-Part.com, which indexes over 200 million components (Car-Part.com, 2026). It's where mechanics and shops go first when they can't find a part locally.

If you're looking for more ways to sell used auto parts, stacking your website with make-and-model pages is one of the simplest first steps.

Does Social Media Work for Salvage Yards?

Facebook Marketplace alone reaches over 1 billion monthly visitors (Meta, 2025). For salvage yards, that's a free storefront in front of a massive audience. Social media won't replace your phone or your walk-in traffic, but it's a low-effort channel that keeps your name in front of local buyers and mechanics.

Facebook Marketplace and Local Groups

List individual parts on Facebook Marketplace with clear photos and specific pricing. Be detailed in titles: "2019 Honda Civic Headlight Assembly, OEM, Tested" outperforms "headlight for sale" every single time.

Join local car enthusiast groups and mechanic forums on Facebook. Don't spam them with listings. Answer questions, help people find parts, and mention your yard when it makes sense. Reputation builds over time, not overnight.

Short Video Walkthroughs

Short videos work. Film a 60-second walkthrough of your yard showing organized shelves, labeled parts, maybe a forklift moving a car. Post it on Facebook or Instagram. No editing needed.

Before-and-after part pulls also perform well. Show the car, the part being removed, then the cleaned part ready for sale. These videos don't need to be polished. Real and honest beats slick and produced every time.

Here's the honest take on social media for salvage yards: results vary. Some yards get steady leads from Facebook. Others post for months and hear nothing. Test one platform for 90 days before you commit more time. If it's not producing calls, move on without guilt.

How Does a Voice Network Work as Marketing?

The US has roughly 9,000 auto recycling businesses (ARA, 2025), and the yards growing fastest aren't just marketing to retail customers. They're connected to other yards through voice parts networks. This isn't traditional marketing, but it functions like word-of-mouth at scale. Every broadcast puts your name in front of 100+ potential trading partners.

Here's how it works. You sit in an always-on conference room with other yards. When someone needs a part, they broadcast the request. Every yard hears it. If you've got the part, you respond. Your name gets heard every time you answer.

Most yard owners think of marketing as reaching end customers, the person who needs a bumper for their Accord. But B2B visibility matters just as much for salvage yard customer acquisition. When other yards know your name and know you respond fast, they broker deals your way. That's referral revenue you didn't create or pay for.

On the Hotline HQ network, yards in California, Texas, Arizona, and Florida broadcast and respond across 12 regional rooms. The investment is minimal: a flat monthly membership and a preconfigured desk phone. No software to learn. Plug in and you're connected.

Want to hear what it sounds like? Listen to a live room. For a deeper look at yard-to-yard collaboration, see how to network with other salvage yards.

How Do Referrals and Repeat Business Compound?

Acquiring a new customer costs five times more than keeping an existing one (Bain & Company via HBR, 2014). For salvage yards, repeat business comes down to trust and making the next purchase easy. These aren't flashy marketing moves, but they compound quietly over months and years.

Warranty Builds Trust

Offer a 30, 60, or 90-day warranty on parts. It costs almost nothing in returns because most used auto parts work fine once installed. But a warranty removes the buyer's biggest hesitation: "What if this doesn't work?" That single question kills more sales than price ever does.

A warranty turns a nervous first-time buyer into a confident repeat customer. It also gives you a real edge over the yard down the road that sells everything as-is. Which yard would you go back to?

Business Cards and the "We'll Find It" Promise

Hand a business card to every customer. It sounds old-fashioned, but it works. That card ends up in a glove box or taped to a shop wall. It's there six months later when they need another part.

The yards we work with that grow the fastest all share one promise: "If we don't have it, we'll find it." When you're part of a parts network, you can actually deliver on that. You turn a lost sale into a brokered one with zero inventory risk.

Pro tip: Track which marketing channel brings each customer. Ask "How did you find us?" at the counter. After 90 days, you'll know exactly where to focus your time and which channels to drop.

Marketing Channels That Waste Your Money

The US vehicle recycling market hit $85.5 billion in 2025 (DataBridge Market Research, 2025). There's real money in this industry. But plenty of yards burn cash on marketing channels that don't fit auto recycling. Here's what to skip so you can redirect that budget to what works.

Print yellow pages: when's the last time you looked something up in a phone book? Your customers haven't recently either. This channel is dead for salvage yards. Radio ads: wrong audience. You pay to reach thousands of listeners who don't need a used auto part today. Compare that to Google, where every searcher already wants what you sell. The cost per actual lead is not even close. Expensive website redesigns: content beats design every time. A $500 website with make-and-model pages and a clear phone number outperforms a $10,000 site with flashy graphics and no useful inventory content. Spend your money on real photos and page content, not on animations and custom themes.

If you're evaluating salvage yard software, remember the distinction: inventory tools help you run your yard, marketing channels help customers find it. Both matter, but they solve different problems. Don't expect a software subscription alone to bring in new customers.

Start Here, This Week

A yard that optimizes its Google Business Profile, builds a basic website, and stays active on one social platform can see walk-in traffic jump 30-50% within months (PYP Accelerator, 2025). Three channels. Zero ad spend. Less than two hours per week.

Start this week. Upload 20 photos to your Google Business Profile. Respond to every pending review. Write your first weekly post. That alone takes about an hour and costs nothing.

After that, build a few make-and-model pages on your site. Test Facebook Marketplace for 90 days. Layer one channel at a time and drop what doesn't produce calls.

posts.bodyHtml:
Disclosure: Hotline HQ publishes this guide. We operate a voice parts network used by 500+ salvage yards. We'll mention it where relevant and flag our own data. Every recommendation stands on its own merits.

Key Takeaways

  • Yards pricing with data hit 20% net margins. Yards pricing from memory average 10% (FinModelsLab, 2025).
  • Every pricing decision needs three inputs: market comparables, part condition grade, and demand signals.
  • Channel matters. Walk-in sales carry the highest margin. eBay requires 13-15% fee padding.
  • A 90-day warranty justifies 20-30% higher prices and builds repeat business.
  • The 90-day rule: if a part hasn't sold in 90 days, drop 10-15% or move it to a discount channel.
You know what the part's worth. Or you think you do. You quote a number, the buyer says yes or walks, and you move on to the next call. That's how most yards price. It's also how most yards leave thousands on the table every month.

Net margins for salvage yards run between 10% and 20% of revenue (FinModelsLab, 2025). That's a wide gap. The difference between the low end and the high end isn't inventory quality or location. It's pricing discipline. The yards at 20% check comparables, grade condition honestly, and adjust for demand. The yards at 10% price from a number they remember from last year.

This guide is for the seller, not the buyer. If you run a yard and you've been pricing by gut, here's a framework that closes the gap.

Why Do Most Yards Underprice Their Parts?

Individual part markups average 50-70% per component (u-pull-it.com, 2025), yet many yards consistently leave 15-25% of that margin uncaptured. The problem isn't greed or lack of effort. It's three habits that feel safe but cost money.

Pricing from memory

You sold a 2018 Camry alternator for $95 six months ago. So you quote $95 again today. But the market moved. Maybe supply dried up. Maybe a new model year made that alternator harder to find. Memory anchors you to yesterday's price, not today's.

How often do you actually check what other yards are charging right now? Car-Part.com indexes over 200 million parts (Car-Part.com, 2026). A two-minute search shows you every yard listing that same alternator and their asking prices. That's your floor and ceiling.

Fear of losing the sale

A customer calls. You have the part. You want the sale. So you quote low to make sure they don't hang up and call the next yard. Sound familiar?

Here's what's actually happening: you're competing against yourself. If your part is in good condition and you can ship or deliver fast, the buyer has reasons to pay more. Speed and reliability carry a premium. Don't undercut yourself before the negotiation starts.

Not knowing your comparables

This one's the root cause. If you don't know what the market rate is, you're guessing. And when you guess, you default to low. No yard owner wants to look greedy, so they err on the side of "reasonable," which usually means 10-20% below what the market would actually bear.

Individual used auto part markups average 50-70% per component according to u-pull-it.com. However, net margins for most salvage yards land between just 10% and 20% of total revenue, per FinModelsLab industry benchmarks. The gap comes from underpricing and overhead, not from weak demand.

What Are the Three Inputs Every Pricing Decision Needs?

Every accurate price sits at the intersection of three data points. Eighty-one percent of auto parts buyers start their search online (PYP Accelerator, 2025), which means pricing data is more accessible than ever, for you and for your buyers. Here's what to check before you quote.

Market comparables

Comparables are what other yards are charging for the same part right now. Not last month, not last year. Right now.

Three places to check:

  1. Car-Part.com - the industry's largest index. Search your part by year, make, model, and interchange number. Note the price range across all listings. Your price should land within that range unless you have a good reason to go higher or lower.
  2. eBay sold listings - not active listings, sold ones. Active listings show what sellers hope to get. Sold listings show what buyers actually paid. Filter by "Sold Items" and you'll see real transaction prices.
  3. Local yard prices - if you're in a market with 5-10 other yards nearby, know their prices. Call them. Check their websites. They're checking yours.

Part condition grading

Not every alternator is the same. A tested unit with a warranty is worth more than one pulled and thrown on a shelf. Use a three-tier grading system:

  • Grade A - Tested, functional, cosmetically clean, sold with a warranty. Commands a 30-50% premium over baseline.
  • Grade B - Functional but shows visual wear. Scuffs, minor surface rust, faded paint. Priced at or near market baseline.
  • Grade C - Untested, sold as-is. No warranty. Priced 30-40% below baseline.

We've seen yards that started grading parts consistently add 12-18% to their average transaction value within three months. The grade gives buyers confidence. Confidence reduces price resistance.

Demand signals

A part with ten requests this week is worth more than one nobody's asked about in two months. Three ways to read demand:

  • Hotline request frequency - what parts are being broadcast most on voice networks? That tells you what buyers can't find.
  • Online search volume - Google Trends and marketplace search data show which parts have growing demand.
  • Seasonal patterns - AC compressors spike in May through July. Heater cores move in October through December. Starters sell more in cold-weather states during winter. Price accordingly.

Eighty-one percent of used auto parts buyers begin their search online, according to PYP Accelerator. This means pricing transparency is high. Yards that use the same public tools, Car-Part.com's 200M+ part index and eBay sold listings, can price with confidence instead of guessing.

The Pricing Formula That Actually Works

Forget complicated spreadsheets. You need one formula with four variables. Here it is.

Base market price x condition multiplier x demand multiplier x channel adjustment = your price

Let's walk through a real example. Say you've got a 2020 Toyota RAV4 LED headlight assembly.

  1. Base market price: You check Car-Part.com. Similar headlights are listed at $180 to $260. The midpoint is $220. That's your base.
  2. Condition multiplier: Yours is Grade A, tested, no hazing, clean lens. Multiplier: 1.3 (30% premium). $220 x 1.3 = $286.
  3. Demand multiplier: RAV4 headlights have been requested three times this week on your network. That's above average. Multiplier: 1.1 (10% bump). $286 x 1.1 = $315.
  4. Channel adjustment: You're selling this walk-in, no fees, no shipping. Multiplier: 1.0 (no adjustment needed). Final price: $315.

That same headlight on eBay? You'd need to account for the 13-15% fee (eBay Seller Center, 2026) plus shipping. So you'd list at $365-$380 to net the same $315.

Most pricing guides tell you to "know your market." That's vague. The formula above gives you a repeatable method. Run every quote through these four variables and you stop guessing. It takes about 90 seconds per part once you get the habit.

How Should You Price Differently by Sales Channel?

eBay charges 13-15% on completed sales (eBay Seller Center, 2026). Walk-in sales cost you nothing in fees. A flat price across all channels means you're overpaying on some and underpricing on others. Here's how to adjust.

Walk-in customers

Your highest-margin channel. No platform fees, no shipping costs, no listing work. The customer's standing in front of you, which means they've already driven to your yard. They're committed. Price at the top of your range. If they push back, you can negotiate. But start high.

eBay and online marketplaces

Factor in fees and shipping before you list. A $200 part nets you $170-$174 after eBay's cut. If that part costs $35 to ship and you're covering it, you're at $135-$139 net. Now compare that to the $200 cash the walk-in customer would've paid. Price your online listings 15-25% higher than your walk-in price to compensate.

Voice networks

Real-time negotiation with other yards who know the market as well as you do. A buyer broadcasting on a network has 100+ yards listening. If your price is out of line, they'll get a better offer in seconds. Price competitively, but don't race to the bottom. Speed and part quality win these sales as much as price does.

On established parts hotlines, response times average about 2 seconds. That speed means the first yard to respond with a fair price often gets the sale. You don't need to be the cheapest. You need to be fast, honest about condition, and priced within the expected range.

Parts locators and brokers

Locators connect you with buyers, but they're working on margin too. Expect them to want prices 30-40% below your direct retail price. Use this channel for parts that have been sitting 60+ days. Don't use it as a primary sales channel or your margins will compress.

eBay charges 13-15% on completed auto parts sales, according to eBay Seller Center. Combined with shipping costs of $35-$200 depending on part size, online channel net revenue can be 25-40% lower than walk-in sales for the same part. Channel-specific pricing eliminates this margin leak.

For a deeper look at how each channel stacks up, see how salvage yards sell more parts.

When Should You Drop the Price vs. Hold?

Owner income at successful yards reaches $200,000 or more, with high performers hitting $400,000+ by year five (FinModelsLab, 2025). Those owners don't hold every part forever. They know when to cut and when to wait. Here's the framework.

The 90-day rule

If a part hasn't sold in 90 days, it's costing you money. Shelf space, cataloging time, and the depreciation that happens as newer model years enter the market. At 90 days, drop the price 10-15% or move the part to a discount channel like a parts locator or a clearance section on your website.

At 180 days, drop again or scrap it. A part sitting for six months at full price isn't an asset. It's overhead.

Seasonal demand curves

Don't drop the price on an AC compressor in March. Demand spikes in May through July. Hold it. Conversely, don't hold a heater core at full price into April. If you missed the winter window, discount it and free up the space for something that'll move.

Model year depreciation

A part from a 2022 vehicle is worth more today than it will be in 2027. As vehicles age, the supply of their parts in salvage increases and the demand stays flat or drops. Parts from vehicles five years old or newer command the best prices. After that, expect 5-10% annual depreciation on most components.

What about rare parts? Different rules. A part from a discontinued model, like a specific trim-level grille or a limited-edition taillight, can actually appreciate. Check the comparables before you assume depreciation applies.

How Does a Warranty Justify Higher Prices?

Yards that offer a 90-day warranty on tested parts report charging 20-30% more than comparable as-is parts, based on pricing patterns visible across Car-Part.com listings (Car-Part.com, 2026). A warranty isn't just a safety net for the buyer. It's a pricing tool for you.

Why warranties work

A buyer choosing between two transmissions, one at $650 as-is and one at $800 with a 90-day warranty, will pick the warranty more often than not. The $150 difference is insurance. For the buyer, it means they won't eat the cost if it fails. For you, it means $150 more per sale.

How often does a tested part actually fail within 90 days? If you're grading honestly and testing properly, returns should run 3-5%. At that rate, you eat one return for every 20-30 sales. The math favors the warranty every time.

Building repeat business

Here's the less obvious benefit. A customer who buys a warrantied part and it holds up will come back. They'll call you first next time. Repeat customers are the cheapest revenue you'll ever earn, no marketing cost, no acquisition cost. Just a phone call from someone who trusts you.

The yards we see growing fastest aren't the ones with the lowest prices. They're the ones with the best reputations for honest grading and standing behind their parts. Price follows trust.

Salvage yard owners can earn $50,000 to over $200,000 annually, with high performers reaching $400,000+ by year five, per FinModelsLab industry data. Pricing discipline, including warranty premiums, condition grading, and channel-specific adjustments, is the primary lever separating these tiers.

Pricing is one of eight strategies that grow a salvage yard business.

FAQ

What is the typical markup on used auto parts?

Individual part markups average 50-70% per component (u-pull-it.com, 2025). That's the gross markup. Net margins for the entire yard land between 10% and 20% of revenue (FinModelsLab, 2025) because overhead, unsaleable vehicles, and underpriced parts eat into that gross number. Pricing with data, not memory, is how you push closer to 20%.

How much do junkyard owners actually make?

Income ranges from $50,000 to over $200,000 depending on yard size, location, and channel mix. High-performing yards with multiple revenue streams, walk-in, online, and network sales, report $400,000+ by year five (FinModelsLab, 2025). The biggest difference between a $50K yard and a $200K yard isn't the inventory. It's pricing strategy and sales channel breadth.

Stacking channels is how you grow that number. Here's how salvage yards sell more parts across five channels.

How do I find out what a used part is worth?

Start with Car-Part.com, which indexes over 200 million parts from yards nationwide. Search your specific part by year, make, and model. Note the price range. Then check eBay's sold listings (not active ones) to see real transaction prices. Adjust for your part's condition grade and your sales channel, and you've got a defensible price.

Not sure which parts command the best margins? See the most profitable parts to pull from a salvage vehicle.

Pricing Is the Fastest Lever You've Got

You can't control how many cars come through the auction. You can't control foot traffic. But you can control how you price every part that leaves your yard. And small improvements, 5% here, 10% there, compound into thousands of dollars per month.

Start with three steps this week:

  1. Check comparables on Car-Part.com for your top 10 parts in stock. Adjust any price that's more than 10% below the market midpoint.
  2. Grade your inventory using the A/B/C system. Mark every part with its grade. Price accordingly.
  3. Listen to a parts hotline for an hour. You'll hear what other yards charge in real time. It's free pricing education. Listen live and hear real pricing conversations between yards.

The yards growing in 2026 aren't the biggest. They're the ones that price deliberately, sell through the right channels, and stand behind what they sell. You've already got the inventory. Now price it like it's worth something.

Not every part in a salvage vehicle is worth your time. A side mirror and a transmission both take roughly 20 minutes of labor. One sells for $50. The other sells for $700. That gap is where profit lives.

Salvage yard net margins run between 10% and 20% on average (FinModelsLab, 2025). The yards on the higher end aren't working harder. They're pulling smarter, focusing labor on parts that combine high resale value, proven demand, and reasonable pull time.

This post ranks the 12 most profitable parts to pull from a salvage vehicle. We've factored in demand frequency, labor effort, and real request volume from yard-to-yard voice networks. Whether you run a one-person operation or manage a crew, this list tells you where to spend your time first.

Key Takeaways

  • Transmissions and engines top the list. High labor, but margins justify every minute.
  • ECU modules and infotainment screens offer the best profit-per-minute: fast pulls, $200 to $800 resale.
  • Network broadcast data shows transmissions are the most requested part, followed by motors and electrical modules ([Hotline HQ network data, 2026]).
  • Use the pull priority formula: sale price x demand frequency / labor minutes.
  • Parts sitting 60 to 90 days sell within two weeks of joining a voice network.

Why Does Pull Priority Matter?

Labor is the biggest controllable cost in a dismantling operation. The average yard pays $15 to $25 per hour in pull labor (IBISWorld, 2025). A part that takes 30 minutes to remove and sells for $80 nets roughly $45 after labor alone. Pull a $600 transmission in that same half hour and you've netted $585.

That math changes everything about how you should organize your day. Most yards pull parts reactively, responding to whatever phone call comes in next. The profitable yards pull proactively. They work through each vehicle in order of part value, touching the car once, pulling high-margin parts first, then circling back for volume items when demand hits.

Here's the real question: if you only had two hours of pull labor today, which parts would you pull first? The list below gives you the answer.

Salvage yards pay $15 to $25 per hour in pull labor on average, according to IBISWorld 2025 industry data. A 30-minute pull on a $600 transmission yields roughly $585 in net labor margin, compared to just $45 on an $80 alternator pulled in the same time. Pull order determines profitability more than inventory size.

The 12 Most Profitable Parts to Pull, Ranked

Profitability isn't just price. It's price relative to pull time, demand frequency, and how quickly you can move the part. Based on market pricing from Car-Part.com's database of 200+ million listings (Car-Part.com, 2026) and real network request data, here are the 12 parts that deliver the best margins for dismantlers.

1. Transmissions - $600 to $1,500+

Transmissions sit at the top for one reason: the margin per unit is massive. A 10-speed automatic from a 2018+ Ford F-150 sells for $800 to $1,500. Rebuilds cost $3,000+, so buyers gladly pay used prices. Pull time runs 45 to 90 minutes with a lift, which is significant. But the math works every time.

Transmissions are the single most requested part across voice parts networks. They lead daily broadcast volume ahead of motors, body panels, and electrical modules.

2. Engines and Motors - $500 to $2,000+

Complete engines deliver the highest per-unit revenue in most yards. A 4-cylinder from a 2018 Toyota Camry runs $500 to $1,200. V8s from full-size trucks push $1,500 to $2,000+. They're heavy, which makes shipping expensive at $150 to $300 freight. That actually helps you. It keeps online competition lower and rewards yards with strong local or network sales channels.

3. ECU and PCM Modules - $200 to $600

Here's your best profit-per-minute pull. An ECU weighs under two pounds, takes 10 to 15 minutes to remove, and sells for $200 to $600 depending on the vehicle. BMW and Mercedes modules sit at the high end because dealer programming fees make new units painfully expensive. Shipping costs almost nothing. These are ideal for online sales and marketplace listings.

4. Catalytic Converters - $150 to $450+

Converters contain platinum, palladium, and rhodium, which gives them intrinsic metal value independent of the auto parts market. A converter from a Toyota Prius runs $300 to $450+. New 2026 state-level regulations have tightened documentation requirements across most states, so keep VIN records tied to every converter you pull (ARA legislative updates, 2026). Legitimate buyers pay more than shady ones.

5. Infotainment and Navigation Screens - $200 to $800

Factory touchscreens are one of the fastest-growing demand categories. A unit from a 2020 Honda CR-V sells for $200 to $500. Luxury brands like BMW, Mercedes, and Audi push $400 to $800. Dealer replacements run $1,500 to $3,000 installed, so used demand stays strong. Pull these early and wrap them carefully. Screen damage kills the value completely.

6. Turbochargers - $300 to $800

Niche, but premium. A turbo from a Ford 2.7L or 3.5L EcoBoost F-150 sells for $300 to $600. Diesel turbochargers from Powerstroke and Duramax trucks push $500 to $800. Check for shaft play before pricing. Clean internals get full price. Detectable wobble drops value by 40% to 60%.

7. Headlight Assemblies - $100 to $400

LED and adaptive headlights from 2017+ vehicles sell consistently. Why? Because new OEM LED headlights from Toyota list at $800 to $1,200 at the dealer. Used assemblies at half that price move fast. Condition is everything: no cracks, no moisture intrusion. A damaged lens drops the value by 50% to 70%.

8. AC Compressors - $100 to $300

Seasonal demand makes these worth watching. Spring and summer are peak months. A compressor from a common vehicle runs $100 to $200. Trucks and luxury vehicles push to $250 to $300. Bench-tested units with a short warranty sell for 30% to 40% more than untested ones.

9. Wheels and Rims - $50 to $300 per wheel

Easy to pull, easy to list, easy to ship. A set of OEM alloy wheels from a 2019 Chevy Silverado runs $150 to $250 per wheel. They photograph well for online listings and don't require complex compatibility matching. Just bolt pattern and size. Four wheels from one truck can add $600 to $1,000 with minimal labor.

10. Power and Heated Seats - $150 to $500

Bulky, yes. But high value. A power/heated driver's seat from a 2019 Ford F-150 sells for $200 to $400. Leather seats from luxury vehicles push higher. These sell best locally or through network channels because shipping a seat is impractical. If you've got local demand, pull them.

11. Alternators - $80 to $200

Quick pulls, steady demand, low risk. A tested alternator from a common vehicle sells for $80 to $150 in about 15 minutes of labor. The margin per unit is modest. But the consistency adds up across dozens of vehicles per month.

12. Starters - $60 to $150

Same logic as alternators. Fast pull, reliable demand, easy to test and tag. Starters from trucks sit at the top of the range. These are the parts you pull after the high-dollar items are already on the shelf. They fill dead time and generate steady baseline revenue.

Car-Part.com indexes over 200 million used auto part listings from yards across North America. Cross-referencing that pricing data with network demand frequency shows transmissions, engines, and ECU modules consistently deliver the highest profit per labor hour for salvage yard dismantlers.

Which Vehicles Yield the Most Profitable Parts?

Full-size trucks consistently produce the highest total parts revenue per vehicle. An average 2017 to 2020 Ford F-150 yields $4,000 to $7,000 in total parts value, according to industry estimates from the Automotive Recyclers Association (ARA, 2025). Late-model Toyota and Honda vehicles offer faster turnover with slightly lower per-unit pricing.

The sweet spot for auction buying is 3 to 7 years old with moderate damage. Front-end collision vehicles are ideal because the transmission, engine, and rear body panels are usually intact. That combination can represent 50% to 60% of the vehicle's total parts value in just three components.

Models to prioritize:

  • Ford F-150, Chevy Silverado, Ram 1500: highest total revenue per vehicle
  • Toyota Camry, Honda Accord, Honda CR-V: fastest turnover, steady demand year-round
  • BMW 3-Series, Mercedes C-Class: high per-part value, but slower movement
  • Subaru Outback, Forester: AWD drivetrain demand keeps prices firm

Don't buy based on the badge. Buy based on the parts you know are selling. If transmissions are moving on your network this week, buy the vehicles that carry the transmissions people are requesting.

How Do You Identify Demand Before You Pull?

The best demand signal isn't a search engine result. It's real buyers asking for real parts in real time. On established voice networks, 300 to 350 part requests broadcast daily, each one representing a buyer ready to purchase ([Hotline HQ network data, 2026]). That's demand data no website or marketplace can replicate at the same speed.

Parts that sat on shelves for 60 to 90 days at isolated yards sell within two weeks of joining a voice network. The difference isn't the part or the price. It's the exposure to active, motivated buyers across dozens of yards simultaneously.

Three practical ways to gauge demand before you start pulling:

  1. Network broadcasts: listen to what yards and shops are requesting. If you hear "2018 Camry transmission" three times in a week, you know exactly what to pull next.
  2. Online search trends: tools like Google Trends show which parts people search for by region and season. AC compressors spike every April. Headlights spike after winter storms.
  3. Your own sales data: track what you sell fastest and what sits. Most yards don't keep this data, and that's a missed opportunity worth fixing.

Have you ever pulled a part, shelved it for three months, and then crushed the car? That's what happens without demand data. It's wasted labor and lost revenue.

The yards pulling the highest margins don't just sell what they have on the shelf. They buy and pull based on what they know people need right now. Demand-first pulling inverts the traditional model, and the yards doing it are growing while their neighbors stay flat.

Voice parts networks generate 300 to 350 broadcast requests per day, according to Hotline HQ 2026 network data. Each broadcast represents a live buyer. Parts that sat unsold for 60 to 90 days at individual yards sell within two weeks of joining a network, confirming that exposure, not pricing, is the primary bottleneck.

The Pull Priority Formula

A pull priority score ranks every part by return on labor. The formula is straightforward: sale price multiplied by demand frequency, divided by pull time in minutes. Research from PYP Accelerator shows that 81% of used auto parts buyers start their search online (PYP Accelerator, 2025). Parts with both high margin and high search visibility score highest.

Here's how it works in practice.

A transmission sells for $800, gets requested 5 times per week on your network, and takes 60 minutes to pull. Score: (800 x 5) / 60 = 66.7.

An alternator sells for $120, gets requested 3 times per week, and takes 15 minutes to pull. Score: (120 x 3) / 15 = 24.

The transmission scores nearly three times higher. Pull it first.

An ECU module sells for $350, gets requested 4 times per week, and takes 12 minutes to pull. Score: (350 x 4) / 12 = 116.7. That's the highest score on the list, which is why ECUs rank third overall despite a lower sticker price.

We've found that yards using any version of this math, even a rough version scribbled on a whiteboard, increase their revenue per labor hour by 15% to 25% within the first quarter. The exact formula matters less than the habit of ranking before pulling.

You don't need software for this. A spreadsheet works. A notebook works. The point is to stop pulling randomly and start pulling with a plan.

ECU modules often score highest because their $200 to $600 price, strong demand, and 12-minute pull time combine to deliver over $100 in priority score, nearly double that of a transmission.

Frequently Asked Questions

What parts sell fastest at a junkyard?

Transmissions, motors, and ECU modules sell fastest because demand is constant and repair shops need them urgently. On voice parts networks, these three categories lead daily broadcast volume ([Hotline HQ network data, 2026]). Headlight assemblies and alternators also move quickly due to high failure rates. Speed of sale depends on pricing, condition, and how many channels you're listed on.

A clean 2017 to 2020 mid-size sedan yields roughly $2,500 to $4,500 in total parts revenue. Full-size trucks run higher, typically $4,000 to $7,000 (ARA industry estimates, 2025). Actual revenue depends on how many parts you pull, test, and sell before the hull goes to scrap metal. Testing and tagging adds 20% to 40% to resale value across every part.

Is it worth pulling small parts like starters and alternators?

Yes, once you've pulled the high-value items first. Starters and alternators cost almost nothing to store, ship cheaply, and sell consistently. A yard that tests and tags these parts can move dozens per week. The margin per unit is modest at $30 to $100 profit per piece, but it adds up. They also fill dead time between big pulls and keep revenue flowing daily.

What to Do Next

The difference between a 10% margin yard and a 20% margin yard isn't luck or location. It's knowing which parts to pull first and having demand data to back those decisions.

Start at the top of this list. Pull transmissions, engines, and ECU modules before you touch anything else on the vehicle. Track what sells and how fast it moves. Use network request data and online search trends to stay ahead of demand, not behind it.

posts.bodyHtml:
Disclosure: Hotline HQ publishes this guide and operates a voice hotline network (Channel 1 below). We've ranked all five channels honestly, including the trade-offs of our own.

Key Takeaways

  • Voice hotlines deliver the fastest response: about 2 seconds per broadcast across 500+ connected yards (Hotline HQ network data, 2026).
  • Online marketplaces add national reach but charge 13-15% fees and move slower (eBay Seller Center, 2026).
  • Walk-in traffic still drives 40-60% of sales at most yards but caps out at a 20-30 mile radius.
  • The most profitable yards stack two to three channels, not just one.
Most salvage yards depend on one or two channels to move inventory. That's a problem when you've got thousands of parts sitting on shelves. The Automotive Recyclers Association estimates roughly 9,000 auto recycling businesses operate across the US (ARA, 2025), all chasing the same buyers. The yards that consistently clear shelves aren't the biggest. They're the ones plugged into more than one sales pipeline.

This guide ranks five channels by speed, reach, and real cost. Voice hotlines, online marketplaces, walk-in traffic, social media, and parts locating services. Each one solves a different problem. You don't need all five. Pick the two or three that fit your yard's size, region, and the kinds of parts you actually stock. We'll cover the pros, cons, and best use case for each, then show you how to stack them.

Why Do Most Yards Rely on a Single Sales Channel?

A typical mid-size yard carries parts from 200 to 500 vehicles at any given time (ARA industry data, 2025). That's thousands of components on shelves, and most yards sell them through walk-ins and repeat phone callers only. Parts sit for months while a buyer one county over never hears about them.

The fix isn't pulling more vehicles. It isn't adding more shelf space. It's connecting what you already have to more buyers through more channels.

Think about it this way. A 2019 Honda Civic front bumper doesn't help anyone if only your regulars know it's there. That bumper has a buyer. Probably more than one. But if your only pipeline is the front counter and a landline, you're invisible to them. Each channel below opens a different path to people who'd buy from you today if they knew you existed.

For a broader look at how channel stacking fits into overall growth strategy, see the yard growth playbook.

How Do Voice Hotlines Help You Sell Faster?

Voice hotlines connect salvage yards on a live conference bridge, organized by region. On established networks, over 500 yards across 12 regional rooms hear every broadcast in real time (Hotline HQ network data, 2026). Average response time: about 2 seconds. Nothing else in this industry moves that fast.

How It Works

Your desk phone stays connected to a regional room, say California or Texas. Someone needs a part, they key up and describe it: "2016 Ford F-150 left headlight assembly." Every yard in the room hears the request live. You have the part? Key up and respond. The two yards arrange the sale directly. No middleman, no listing fees, no waiting.

Compare that to spending 30 or 60 minutes calling yards one by one. On a hotline, the broadcast goes out and you've got an answer in seconds. The busiest rooms see 300 to 350 broadcasts per day (Hotline HQ network data, 2026). That's 300+ chances to sell a part already sitting on your shelf, without lifting a finger to list it.

How does that volume break down in practice? A single California room has over 200 active yards, producing the highest broadcast density of any US voice parts network. When a request goes out, your odds of having the part and hearing about it in real time are dramatically higher than any other channel.

Pros

  • Fastest time-to-sale of any channel (seconds, not hours)
  • One broadcast reaches 100+ yards at once
  • Flat monthly cost, no per-sale commission
  • Real-time means no stale inventory data
  • Two-way value: sell parts and source parts on the same channel

Cons

  • Reach is limited to yards on your regional room
  • Requires someone near the phone during business hours
  • You respond to live requests rather than listing inventory for passive discovery

Best For

Yards doing steady daily volume that want the fastest path to a sale. The always-on model catches demand in the background while your team does other work. If you're curious how these networks evolved from CB radios to modern SIP bridges, read the yard networking guide.

Hotline HQ network data shows the California room alone has over 200 active yards, generating 300-350 daily broadcasts, the highest broadcast density of any US voice parts network.

Can Online Marketplaces Move Parts at Scale?

Platforms like eBay Motors and Car-Part.com give dismantlers access to millions of buyers. Car-Part.com lists over 200 million parts from yards nationwide (Car-Part.com, 2026). No other single channel puts you in front of that many eyeballs. But broader reach comes with real trade-offs: fees, stale data, and a slower sales cycle.

How It Works

You photograph, describe, and price each part individually. Then you wait. A buyer searches, finds your listing, and completes the purchase. That cycle takes hours to days. Because inventory updates are manual, buyers sometimes try to order parts you've already sold or pulled. Stale listings create customer service headaches and damage your seller rating over time.

eBay charges roughly 13% to 15% on completed parts sales when you combine listing fees and payment processing (eBay Seller Center, 2026). Car-Part.com uses a subscription model instead. Either way, you're paying for reach. The question is whether the volume justifies the cost.

For most yards with high-value inventory and someone to manage listings, the answer is yes. A $400 ECU module that sells on eBay nets you roughly $340 after fees. That same ECU sitting unseen on your shelf nets you nothing.

Pros

  • National buyer pool, millions of potential customers
  • Passive sales: listings work while you're closed
  • Strong for high-value, easily shipped parts (ECUs, headlights, sensors)
  • Buyers come pre-qualified, they searched for that exact part

Cons

  • Fees eat 13-15% of every sale on eBay
  • Inventory data goes stale between manual updates
  • Time-intensive to photograph and list each part
  • Price competition across national sellers compresses margins

Best For

Yards with dedicated office staff to manage listings. Works especially well for specialty, rare, or high-value parts where national buyers will pay shipping and a premium. If you need help figuring out which parts are worth the listing effort, check the most profitable parts guide.

What's the Real Ceiling on Walk-In Traffic?

Walk-in customers provide steady, predictable revenue at most yards. For many small-to-mid-size dismantlers, repeat local buyers account for 40% to 60% of total parts sales (industry estimate, figures vary by region). This is your highest-margin channel. Zero fees, zero shipping costs, zero middlemen. But it caps your buyer pool at roughly a 20 to 30 mile radius.

How It Works

Walk-in volume depends on three things: location, signage, and local reputation. A yard on a busy road near body shops and mechanics draws traffic naturally. A yard tucked behind an industrial park? Not so much.

You can improve numbers with better signage, a solid Google Business Profile, and word-of-mouth referrals from the shops you've treated right over the years. But there's a ceiling, and you'll hit it. You'll never reach the body shop two states away that needs the exact part gathering dust on your shelf.

Walk-in traffic works as a baseline. It keeps the lights on. It can't be your only play if you want to grow.

Pros

  • Zero fees, zero commissions, zero shipping costs
  • Cash transactions with fast payment
  • Builds long-term repeat customer relationships
  • Customers inspect parts in person, reducing returns

Cons

  • Geographically limited to a 20-30 mile radius
  • Volume varies by weather, day of week, and season
  • Doesn't help move parts that local buyers aren't asking for
  • Hard to grow past the local market ceiling

Best For

Every yard benefits from walk-in traffic. It's your floor revenue. But relying on it alone means you're invisible to 99% of potential buyers. For strategies to bring more walk-in traffic through the gate, check the salvage yard marketing playbook.

Yards we've worked with that added even one additional channel, typically a voice hotline, saw parts that had sat for 60 to 90 days sell within the first two weeks after connecting.

Is Social Media Worth the Effort for Parts Sales?

Facebook Marketplace and local buy-sell groups have become a free sales channel for yards willing to post consistently. Meta reports Facebook Marketplace reaches over 1 billion monthly visitors worldwide (Meta, 2025). Parts with clear photos sell, especially common items like engines, transmissions, and body panels. But results swing wildly from week to week.

How It Works

Post a photo with year, make, model, and price. Buyers message you directly. Some yards post 10 to 20 parts per week and see consistent inquiries. Others post the same volume and hear crickets. Facebook's algorithm decides who sees your listing. You don't control that, and it shifts without warning.

What about make-specific Facebook groups? They can work surprisingly well for enthusiast parts. A rare JDM engine or a classic Mustang fender gets more attention in a dedicated group than on any parts database. But the effort-to-return ratio is unpredictable. You might sell three parts from one post and nothing from the next twenty.

Pros

  • Free to list, no subscription or transaction fees
  • Reaches local consumers outside traditional yard networks
  • Make-specific groups attract serious, knowledgeable buyers
  • Photos and video help sell condition-sensitive parts

Cons

  • Reach is entirely algorithm-dependent and changes without notice
  • Time-consuming to photograph, post, and respond to messages
  • Attracts tire-kickers, lowballers, and no-shows
  • No inventory management: sold parts stay posted until you remove them
  • Not designed for B2B yard-to-yard transactions

Best For

Yards with retail-friendly or specialty inventory and someone willing to manage posts consistently. Treat social media as a supplement, not a primary channel. It works best in metro areas where the local Facebook group population is large enough to generate real demand.

Social media produces meaningful parts sales almost exclusively for yards in metro areas with large local Facebook group populations. Rural yards rarely see real volume from this channel because the buyer density isn't there. If your zip code has fewer than 50,000 people, your time is better spent on a voice hotline or marketplace.

What About Parts Locating Services?

Parts locators act as middlemen between end buyers, usually repair shops, and salvage yards. Companies like PartsHotlines.com search databases of over 1,000 yards to match requests with available inventory. The convenience is real, but so is the margin hit: locators typically pay 30% to 40% below your direct-sale price (industry data).

How It Works

The locator handles the search and the customer relationship. You get a call or order for a specific part at a set price. Most locators charge a per-request fee or take a commission on completed sales. You're selling wholesale, plain and simple.

The other issue is speed. Database-driven locating relies on inventory records that may be days or weeks old. By the time a locator matches your part to a buyer, a yard on a live network may have already closed that deal. Locators fill a gap, but they're not where you want to send your best inventory first.

Pros

  • Passive: the locator finds buyers for you
  • No listing, marketing, or sales effort on your end
  • Surfaces demand from repair shops that don't know your yard exists

Cons

  • You sell at wholesale, typically 30-40% below direct prices
  • No relationship with the end customer
  • Dependent on the locator's network and effort
  • Stale database records can slow the match process

Best For

Moving slow-turning inventory that isn't selling through other channels. If a part has sat for 90 days with no matches on the hotline or your marketplace listings, a locator sale at a discount beats zero revenue. To make sure you're not giving away margin unnecessarily, review the pricing strategy guide.

Which Channels Should You Stack Together?

The most active sellers on established voice networks typically run two to three channels at once (Hotline HQ network data, 2026). No single channel covers all the demand for your parts. Here's a framework for picking the right mix based on your biggest constraint.

Short on time? A voice hotline is the lowest-effort active channel. Plug in a phone, listen, respond when you've got the part. No listings, no photos, no algorithm games. Short on staff? They won't scale past your zip code, but they keep parts moving while you build up.

The Stack That Works for Most Mid-Size Yards

  1. Voice hotline as the primary channel for speed and daily volume
  2. Online marketplace (Car-Part.com or eBay) for national reach on high-value parts
  3. Walk-in traffic as the local baseline with the highest margins

Add Facebook for specialty or enthusiast parts when you've got the staff time. Use locating services as a last resort for inventory that hasn't moved through faster channels.

For a side-by-side look at the software that ties these channels together, check the salvage yard software comparison.

Picking Your First New Channel

The parts on your shelves aren't dead weight. They're unseen. Every one of them has a buyer somewhere. The only question is whether you're connected to enough channels to find that buyer before the part rusts out or the model ages off the road.

Start with one new channel. Get it running, measure results for 30 days, then decide if a third makes sense. Most yards see the biggest jump when they add their second channel. Going from one to two changes the economics of your entire shelf. The third channel adds incremental reach. The first new one is the one that changes everything.

Don't try to launch all five at once. You'll spread your team too thin and none of them will work properly. Pick the channel that fills the biggest gap in your current setup. If you're only doing walk-ins, a voice hotline adds speed and regional reach overnight. If you're already on a hotline, an eBay store adds national visibility on your high-margin parts.

Ready to add a voice channel to your yard? Sign up free and get on the line with 500+ dismantlers across 12 regional rooms.

FAQ

What is the fastest way to sell used auto parts?

Voice hotline networks deliver the fastest yard-to-yard sales. A single broadcast reaches 100+ yards, and the average response takes about 2 seconds (Hotline HQ network data, 2026). Online marketplaces reach more individual buyers but responses take hours to days. For most yards, stacking a hotline with one marketplace channel covers both speed and national reach.

Can small salvage yards compete with large dismantlers on volume?

Yes. Network access matters more than yard size. A small yard on a voice hotline with 200+ members hears every request a larger yard hears. If you have the part, the buyer doesn't care how big your lot is. Stack two or three channels and a 10-car-a-week yard can outsell a 50-car operation stuck on walk-ins alone.

How many sales channels does a salvage yard actually need?

Two to three is the sweet spot for most mid-size yards. A voice hotline for speed, an online marketplace for national reach, and walk-in traffic for local margin. Adding a fourth channel like social media makes sense only when you have staff time to keep it active. Fewer channels done well beats five channels done poorly.
